title: Artificial Slack - On the Efficiency Rebound Effects of Artificial Intelligence in Organizations
affiliations: VU University Amsterdam - Faculty of Social Sciences

detail.title: Artificial Slack - On the Efficiency Rebound Effects of Artificial Intelligence in Organizations
detail.abstract: Applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) are increasingly transforming work in organizations, ushering into a new division of labour between humans and machines. As AI systems can operate like a co-worker and take over an unprecedented range of tasks they are commonly regarded as a source of greater organizational efficiency. However, as this article argues, AI uses can lead to various efficiency rebound effects as they can engender new forms of wastefulness. These are rooted in a novel kind of abundance that stems from AI expanding organizational task performance both in breadth and volume. Specifically, wastefulness can result from AI-based induced demand, amplified siloing, slack in knowledge management, and proliferation of red tape. AI is thus likely to have negative effects on efficiency unless its implementation is carefully managed. The discussion points to possible ways of shaping AI in the future organizational division of labour to avoid novel forms of wastefulness.

title: Strategic Proposal: Cognitive Blind Spots in Security Frameworks – A Priority for the 2026 BCS Agenda
affiliations: University of Liverpool

detail.title: Strategic Proposal: Cognitive Blind Spots in Security Frameworks – A Priority for the 2026 BCS Agenda
detail.abstract:
This presentation was delivered at the BCS IT Leaders Forum Symposium on November 13, 2025, as a topic submission for the institute's 2026 strategic work programme.

The proposal argues that the 2026 agenda must address a critical gap in current resilience strategies: the "cognitive blind spots" embedded in standard security frameworks. Drawing on cross-sector analysis, the deck demonstrates how cognitive biases — specifically Anchoring Bias and Overconfidence Bias — can lead to governance failures even when "best practices" are strictly followed.

The presentation highlights a "temporal mismatch" where annual governance cycles lag behind weekly adversary evolution. It further warns that emerging AI governance standards (such as ISO 42001) are currently replicating these structural flaws, leading to exponential risk drift.

To correct this "direction of travel," the proposal suggests prioritising Bias-Resistant Governance in the 2026 roadmap. It outlines three specific pillars for development:

- Flow Limits: Moving from cycle-based to flow-based governance (using Kanban principles) to prevent anchoring on outdated plans.
- Shared Intelligence: Establishing AI-specific threat intelligence ecosystems (extending STIX/TAXII) to create missing feedback loops.
- Bias Checkpoints: Institutionalising structured challenges to assumptions to counter organisational inertia.

Based on Research Paper: Shabad, Vsevolod 'Cognitive Blind Spots in Security Frameworks: From Cybersecurity to AI Governance (2025)'. SSRN Working Paper No. 5525340. Available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5525340

title: A Systematic Mapping Study of Software Product Management for Business Applications (Preprint)

detail.title: A Systematic Mapping Study of Software Product Management for Business Applications (Preprint)
detail.abstract:
CONTEXT: This systematic literature review was driven by the main research question \textit{``What challenges has software engineering research addressed for Software Product Management with a particular focus on business applications?''}. The current version of the International Software Product Management Association (ISPMA) framework (version 2.0) was used to conduct a systematic mapping study to identify areas that have been researched extensively, as well as areas with limited prior research, including complementary topics at the borders of the defined Software Product Management (SPM) domain.

OBJECTIVES: Creation of a question-led systematic mapping study in the area of software product management with focus on business applications.

METHODS: The main research question results in a generic search request that was used to search in two large scientific databases, SCOPUS and Web of Science, for existing publications. After identification of duplicates 162 articles have been screened in a first step on the level of their title. 12 records have been excluded on that level. In the second round the remaining 150 publications have been screened based on their abstract. Again 24 articles have been excluded. Finally, 126 studies remained, and a detailed manuscript review has been done, supported by the ``DistillerSR''\copyright \, online tool that handles all articles and allow a form-based data extraction. The extracted data has been exported to comma-separated text-files (csv-files) and the source data has been analyzed with Microsoft Excel. Results have been documented in the literature review, figures give an overview of the extracted data, detail information is listed in tables in the appendix or as electronic supplement.

RESULTS:  The literature review shows that much research in the last decades has been done in areas of the ISPMA framework -- and also in the wider area of Software Product Management. Especially in the ISPMA-areas of Requirement Engineering much research exists: 31.0~\% of all studies that have been screened in the literature review remain to Product Requirement Engineering and 15.9~\% in addition to Detailed Requirements Engineering.  Within the ISPMA core focus field of ``Product Planning'', the ``Product Requirements Engineering'' functional area is the most researched, accounting for nearly half of all publications in the entire functional area. In most cases, these studies have a short-term operational focus. 

CONCLUSION: The structured screening of the literature review suggests that researchers have described different aspects of the functional areas of roadmapping and release planning. For further research it will be interesting to take a closer look at dealing with the complexity of the software product roadmap process and the associated release planning process. The critical part of feature prioritization in practice could also be of interest for further research. In addition, the organization of Software Product Management for large or medium-sized business applications with focus on standard software products might be worth to put a spotlight on. Last but not least, the decision structure regarding the inclusion and exclusion of features in software products seems to be an area where further research may be relevant.

detail.abstract: In this special issue we explore the role that libraries, librarians, and information professionals can play in advancing AI literacy in our workplaces and communities.  AI literacy is a broad term meant to encompass educating users about AI use, production, and evaluation; however, as we can see there is no commonly agreed upon definition as of yet.  The included literature reflects common similarities in the need to incorporate AI literacy into our ongoing work as librarians and educators, while also recognizing that libraries serving such a wide base of communities will need to lead literacy efforts that are uniquely tailored to the populations they serve.

detail.title: Technology Diffusion in Emerging Markets: A Systematic Examination of Complementarities
detail.abstract: We study how technology diffusion differs in emerging markets through the lens of complementarities. Because adoption requires complementary assets such as skills, implementation capability, and access to external knowledge, diffusion depends on technology-complement fit. We build a patents-to-postings measurement framework linking 31 million job postings with Chinese patents and identify 3,269 technologies visible in both invention and labor demand. Using LLM-based, retrieval-augmented text analysis to classify occupations and skills, we characterize technologies' complement requirements and measure diffusion as the geographic broadening of technology-related postings across Chinese cities. Technologies originate in a small set of hubs and broaden over time, but broadening is slower for technologies that require scarcer complements, including those implemented in higher-skill jobs, those that are more upstream in the innovation chain, and those more dependent on U.S. prior art. COVID-19 slows diffusion, while U.S. Entity List sanctions are associated with faster diffusion consistent with localization. The findings imply that technology adoption in emerging markets depends critically on the availability and coordination of complementary assets.

title: Be Ready for the Future? An Economic Analysis of Over-the-Air Software Upgrades in the Automotive Industry
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Information Systems, Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - School of Management, University of North Texas and State University of New York (SUNY) - Management Science and Systems

detail.title: Be Ready for the Future? An Economic Analysis of Over-the-Air Software Upgrades in the Automotive Industry
detail.abstract: As software-driven innovation becomes central to product differentiation in the automotive industry, manufacturers are leveraging over-the-air (OTA) upgrades to deliver feature enhancements. Unlike hardware upgrades that require physically delivered service, software upgrades are information products that can be deployed remotely via OTA, fundamentally reshaping firms’ product design and intertemporal pricing decisions. We investigate how automotive manufacturers should design and price their products over time when software-enabled features can be unlocked through OTA upgrades. We develop a two-period analytical framework to examine and compare two product design and pricing strategies: the traditional versioning model, in which hardware and software upgrades are bundled and introduced in the second period, and the emerging OTA upgrades model, in which hardware is pre-installed in the first period and software upgrades are activated via over-the-air updates in the second period. Our analysis highlights two key advantages of OTA upgrades. First, the tech-savviness segmentation effect allows firms to use software pricing in the second period as an additional lever to achieve more fine-grained consumer segmentation within the same period. Second, the adoption time segmentation effect eliminates consumers’ incentives to delay purchase, ensuring a clean separation of higher-valuation consumers in the first period from lower-valuation consumers in the second period. This bilateral segmentation enables the manufacturer to mitigate price distortions and capture value more effectively. However, the OTA upgrades model requires pre-installing upgrade-ready hardware, which increases production costs, and thus it only outperforms traditional versioning when the cost of developing software is moderate. Finally, we examine welfare implications. Although some consumers view OTA upgrades as unfair, believing they pay for latent features they may never use, it can nevertheless generate consumer benefits through enhanced access to upgrades or lower prices of the base vehicle, creating a “Win-Win” outcomes in a wide range of market conditions. Our findings contribute to the literature on technology-enabled new product design by formalizing the economic trade-offs inherent in the OTA upgrades model. In addition, we provide actionable guidance for auto manufacturers on how to structure OTA upgrades.

detail.abstract: The pace of adoption of generative AI has been groundbreaking—faster than the adoption of personal computers and the internet. detail.abstract: The present study examines how sustainable marketing practices shape gastronomic experience, visitor satisfaction and destination loyalty in Turkish ecotourism destinations (Gaziantep, Izmir, and Konya) selected for their distinct sustainability dynamics, namely gastronomy, slow living, and agriculture. Data collected from 380 tourists were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings indicate that the influence of sustainability practices is predominantly manifested through experiential factors. Specifically, social and cultural dimensions of sustainability practices have a significant and positive impact on the gastronomic experience, whereas environmental and economic dimensions exhibit limited associations. The gastronomic experience exerts a direct and significant influence on visitor satisfaction and destination loyalty; however, satisfaction plays a modest mediating role in the formation of loyalty. The concept of social sustainability has emerged as a significant predictor of satisfaction and loyalty, with the gastronomic experience being a notable influencer in this regard. Overall, the results suggest that sustainability-related actions are most consequential when translated into tangible, community-embedded gastronomic experiences that visitors can directly perceive; this underscores the importance of experiential and cultural strategies for destination management and offers practical insights for tourism marketers and policymakers.

title: What Happens When Dating Goes Online? Evidence from U.S. Marriage Markets and Health Outcomes
affiliations: UCL School of Management, University of Michigan Ross School of Business and University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: What Happens When Dating Goes Online? Evidence from U.S. Marriage Markets and Health Outcomes
detail.abstract: This paper studies how online dating platforms have impacted marital outcomes, assortative matching, and sexually transmitted disease (STD) rates in the United States. We construct county-level measures of online dating usage using data from website-based platforms (2002-2013) and mobile app-based platforms (2017-2023). Leveraging county-level variation and an instrumental variable strategy, we show in the desktop era, a 1% increase in online dating sessions raises divorce rates by 0.50%, while in the mobile era, a 1% increase in online dating activity lowers marriage and divorce rates by 0.40% and 0.33%, respectively. We also document shifts in assortative matching. Desktop sites reduce sorting along education and employment dimensions, whereas mobile sites reduce sorting by employment, but increase sorting by race. Across both eras, we find no evidence that greater online dating usage increases average STD rates. Average effects are negative or statistically insignificant, but are positive for some subpopulations. We develop a search and matching model where technological changes impact search costs, market size, and market noise can explain our empirical findings.

title: Software Product Management for Business Applications with Special Focus on Standard Software Products

detail.title: Software Product Management for Business Applications with Special Focus on Standard Software Products
detail.abstract:
CONTEXT: The long-term evolution of standard software products with a high functional scope occurs in constantly changing markets. Various stakeholders try to enforce their interests in the short and long term in developing business applications. However, given limited development resources and technological improvements, prioritizing the most important requirements is necessary. These requirements must align with corporate and product strategies and be integrated into decision processes for further software development in a value-based manner. These conditions pose great challenges for software product managers.

OBJECTIVES: Creation of a new integrated model for standard software product development.

METHODS:The research design of this study includes a systematic mapping study that examines the area of Software Product Management (SPM) and describes the functional areas of road mapping and release planning in more detail. Subsequently, a multiple case study of three Austrian standard software vendors of different sizes was conducted. The data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis.

RESULTS: On the basis of 126 systematically identified studies \cite[under review]{Salzmann2025} and 21 additional studies and a supplemented by snowball search, two hypothetical models of software product development for the production of standard software products were designed. One of the developed hypothetical models was iteratively improved by the three cases of the multiple case study and extended to an integrated model for standard software product development. This final model was validated by practitioners in five standard software companies.

CONCLUSION: The integrated model of software product creation describes the quasi-continuous flow of external and internal requirements, which, depending on external and internal drivers, lead to the further development of standard software applications. The tasks of software product managers and their interdisciplinary teams as well as the decisions of stakeholders are essentially determined by three temporal levels: the long-term product vision, the medium-term product roadmap and the short-term release plan.

title: Should We Tax Robots? Innovation, Productivity, and the Future of Fiscal Policy
affiliations: University of Colorado at Denver - Department of Finance

detail.title: Should We Tax Robots? Innovation, Productivity, and the Future of Fiscal Policy
detail.abstract: Rapid advances in automation, artificial intelligence, and robotics are transforming labor markets, productivity, and income distribution. As machines increasingly substitute for human labor, a growing policy debate has emerged around whether robots should be taxed. Proponents argue that a robot tax could slow labor displacement, fund social safety nets, and reduce inequality, while opponents warn that such a tax would stifle innovation, reduce productivity growth, and weaken global competitiveness. This paper critically evaluates the economic rationale for taxing robots. We argue that while concerns about inequality and labor displacement are valid, taxing robots directly is a blunt and potentially counterproductive policy tool. Instead, we propose an alternative framework that focuses on taxing economic rents, capital income, and excess profits generated by automation, while simultaneously investing in human capital, reskilling, and innovation. The paper contributes to the literature by clarifying conceptual definitions of "robots," analyzing dynamic general equilibrium effects of robot taxation, and offering a forward-looking fiscal policy framework for the age of intelligent machines.

title: Regulatory Compliance and Business Sustainability of Ukay-Ukay Stores in San Jose City, Nueva Ecija

detail.title: Regulatory Compliance and Business Sustainability of Ukay-Ukay Stores in San Jose City, Nueva Ecija
detail.abstract: The study described the regulatory compliance and business sustainability of ukay-ukay stores of Calendar Year 2025 in San Jose City, Nueva Ecija. The quantitative-descriptive research design was used to conduct a survey of fifty-seven (57) store owners who were selected using a purposive sampling. Data regarding the profiles of respondents, regulatory compliance in business registration and licensing, tax liabilities, custom and importation, consumer protection, and fire and safety standards, such as business sustainability in business operations, profitability, and longterm sustainability, were collected using a validated researcher-developed questionnaire. The analysis was carried out by counts, percentages, means, and standard deviations. The results revealed that most of the respondents were women aged between 30 and 60, married, college graduates, and had been operating their businesses averagely a period of six years hence their operations were not very volatile. Findings also indicated moderate adherence to regulatory standards and typical exercised business sustainability measures, but flaws were identified in productivity strategies, investment in innovation and ability to generate consistent profits. The key difficulties included stiff competition with other brick and mortar and online retailers, scarcity of facilities, and inability to pass regulatory processes. The paper concludes that though the ukayukay enterprises are favorable to the local economy and have moderate compliance and sustainability levels, there is a need to have more efforts in terms of governmental support and capacity-building interventions intended to enhance the performance and resilience of the enterprises in the long term.

title: Beyond Binary Positions: Making Space for Critical and Reflexive GenAI Integration in Qualitative Research
affiliations: , Monash University,  and Portland State University

detail.title: Beyond Binary Positions: Making Space for Critical and Reflexive GenAI Integration in Qualitative Research

keywords: Ethical Use of AI for Qualitative Research
Open Letter Critical and Reflexive Discussion on the Use of GenAI
Rejecting the Use of GenAI for Reflexive Qualitative Analysis

detail.abstract:
We write as qualitative researchers to respond to an open letter - recently circulating on LinkedIn and now published in the journal of  Qualitative Inquiry (Jowsey et al., 2025a), opposing the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in reflexive qualitative research. We have also submitted our response to Qualitative Inquiry and are currently awaiting a decision on whether our open letter will be considered for publication.

The open letter by Jowsey et al. calls for the categorical exclusion of generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) from reflexive qualitative research. While we acknowledge the ethical and socio-technical concerns that motivate this position, we respectfully contest the conclusion that GenAI is inherently incompatible with meaning-based methodologies.

We believe that rejecting the technology in its entirety risks closing off methodological evolution, misunderstanding current practices, and isolating qualitative research from broader epistemic developments. 

Furthermore, a blanket rejection of GenAI in qualitative research can reinforce a problematic binary framing between pro- versus anti-AI, or ethical versus non-ethical positions, which may risk marginalizing in-between efforts that develop, design, and apply GenAI in ethical and responsible manners. Our stance is to refuse to side with either an absolutist anti-AI position (i.e., an outright rejection of all potential uses of GenAI) or an uncritical pro-AI enthusiasm (i.e., accepting that anything goes as long as it increases efficiency). 

We believe in the diversity and flexibility of qualitative research practices where researchers can engage with GenAI while remaining reflexive, ethical, and responsible. We therefore advocate for a position grounded in critical engagement, methodological literacy, and ethical responsibility. GenAI, like any other technologies including computer-assisted qualitative data analysis software (CAQDAS), when used critically and under close researcher leadership and control, can serve as a legitimate analytic support within reflexive qualitative inquiry. 

We therefore support:

  • continued methodological development exploring GenAI as a reflexive analytic aid, with methodological groundings and critical evaluation of its capabilities and limitations; 
  • maintenance of human interpretive and reflexive agency in all analytic decisions, positioning GenAI as a tool or an assistant under researcher control rather than an autonomous agent;
  • transparency and reflexivity in the design, implementation, monitoring, evaluation, and reporting of GenAI-supported analyses;
  • collective action to reduce environmental and labour harms that targets big tech companies rather than individual qualitative researchers who critically and reflexively experiment, apply, or use GenAI in their work.

We invite colleagues from across discipline and methodological traditions to participate in constructive dialogue about how qualitative research can engage productively and responsibly with emerging computational tools.

title: The Impact of Wars on International Marketing Strategies

detail.title: The Impact of Wars on International Marketing Strategies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: by self

detail.abstract:
This study examines the impact of wars on international marketing strategies, with a particular focus on how armed conflicts influence consumer behavior and the overall marketing operations of organizations. The research aims to provide an in-depth understanding of the challenges faced by companies during periods of war and to explore how marketing strategies can be adapted to overcome these obstacles.

The study adopts a descriptive and analytical methodology supported by quantitative data collection tools to assess the effects of war on the four elements of the marketing mix: product, price, distribution, and promotion. Structured questionnaires were designed and distributed to a targeted sample in order to collect primary data. The collected data were subsequently analyzed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS).

The main findings indicate that wars cause significant disruptions in global supply chains, directly affecting distribution channels and pricing strategies as a result of fluctuations in production costs and exchange rates. These disruptions place additional pressure on companies to reassess their operational efficiency and logistical resilience in unstable environments.

Furthermore, the study reveals that wartime conditions compel organizations to adjust their promotional and communication strategies in response to the social and economic transformations caused by armed conflicts. There is a noticeable shift toward more cautious messaging, increased reliance on digital marketing channels, and a growing emphasis on sustainability and ethical considerations in marketing practices.

Based on these findings, the study recommends that companies diversify their product portfolios and marketing strategies in order to enhance organizational resilience and adaptability during periods of conflict. Such diversification enables firms to mitigate risks, maintain market presence, and respond more effectively to rapidly changing consumer needs under unstable conditions.

detail.abstract: The widespread adoption of social media has transformed the way individuals access information, communicate ideas and make financial decisions. In recent years social media platforms such as Instagram, Twitter, YouTube, TikTok, Facebook etc have emerged as major sources of investment related content often shared through influencers in form of short videos, discussion threads, review videos and trending posts. This study examines the influence of social media on the investment decisions of retail investors and evaluates whether such influence leads to positive or negative outcomes. Using a quantitative surveybased research design primary data was collected from 120 respondents with varying levels of investment experience. The findings reveal that social media plays a significant role in shaping investment behaviour, with a large proportion of respondents reporting that they have acted on investment information encountered online. Emotional factors, particularly fear of missing out (FOMO) were found to strongly influence decision making and often reduced the likelihood of careful verification. While social media contributes to greater awareness and participation in financial markets the results suggest that it also encourages impulsive and short-term investment decisions which may result in unsatisfactory outcomes. This study contributes to existing literature by providing practical, investor focused evidence on the behavioural impact of social media and highlights the importance of financial literacy, responsible content creation and cautious decision making in the digital investment environment.

title: Integrating Knowledge Management into Supply Chain Due Diligence: A Governance-Oriented Framework for Compliance, ESG, and Risk Mitigation

detail.title: Integrating Knowledge Management into Supply Chain Due Diligence: A Governance-Oriented Framework for Compliance, ESG, and Risk Mitigation
detail.abstract: This article examines the integration of knowledge management into supply chain due diligence as a strategic instrument of corporate governance, compliance, and risk mitigation in complex regulatory environments. It argues that traditional due diligence models-largely centered on formal controls, periodic audits, and contractual safeguards-are increasingly insufficient to address systemic, diffuse, and transnational risks associated with global supply chains, particularly those related to ESG agendas, human rights, anti-corruption, and third-party liability. Adopting an interdisciplinary approach that combines law, corporate governance, compliance, and organizational studies, the article proposes a conceptual framework that repositions due diligence as a dynamic system of organizational learning. It contends that effective supply chain governance depends on the ability of organizations to capture, structure, share, and continuously reintegrate knowledge derived from audits, investigations, incidents, and stakeholder interactions. The article concludes that embedding knowledge management into due diligence processes transforms compliance from a reactive control mechanism into a forward-looking system of organizational intelligence.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study explores the mediating role of financial policies in the relationship between corporate governance and agency costs to introduce a model-based measure for agency costs, which accounts for the residuals of the regression of Free Cash Flow (FCF) on growth opportunities. Design/methodology/approach: To achieve this goal, the study analyzed the direct and indirect effects of corporate governance on agency costs using data from up to 400 companies and employed structural equations modeling. Agency costs were measured as the error term of the the regression of free cash flow on growth opportunities. Findings: The results indicate that the new measure proposed in this study for assessing agency costs enabled a more coherent exploration of the indirect effects of corporate governance on agency costs. Specifically, after implementing this measure, the indirect effect of corporate governance on agency costs through dividend payouts was confirmed. Furthermore, the robustness checks conducted affirm the validity of the findings. Implications: The findings enhance the capacity of institutional shareholders to quantify the agency costs imposed by managers, thereby improving the quality of corporate governance. Originality: This research is original in its development of a novel model-based measure for assessing agency costs, which facilitates a more accurate evaluation of the impact of corporate governance on these costs.

title: The Influence of Green Awareness on Attitude Toward Green Products Mediated by Environmental Concern, Perceived Benefit, and Perceived Price on Environmentally Friendly Detergent Products

detail.title: The Influence of Green Awareness on Attitude Toward Green Products Mediated by Environmental Concern, Perceived Benefit, and Perceived Price on Environmentally Friendly Detergent Products
detail.abstract: This study aims to determine the influence of Green Awareness on Attitude Toward Green Product on environmentally friendly detergent products mediated by Environmental Concern, Perceived Benefit, and Perceived Price. This study was conducted on consumers of environmentally friendly detergent products in the Greater Jakarta area, involving 115 respondents. Data were collected using a questionnaire and analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The results of the study show that Green Awareness has a positive and significant effect on Environmental Concern, Perceived Benefit, and Perceived Price. These three dimensions significantly mediate the influence of Green Awareness on Attitude Toward Green Product. These findings underscore the important role of consumer awareness and price perception in shaping positive attitudes toward environmentally friendly products. The practical implications of this research suggest that companies should manage price perceptions and enhance environmental education to encourage broader purchase of green products.

detail.abstract: Over the past two decades, marketing automation has evolved from simple tools for campaign management into a sophisticated ecosystem powered by AI, big data, and predictive analytics. This transformation enables firms to manage omnichannel campaigns, personalize content at scale, and optimize decision-making in real time, shifting marketing from intuition-based practices to data-driven strategies. Beyond operational efficiency, marketing automation acts as a strategic resource that reshapes customer relationships, competitive dynamics, and organizational performance. Its implementation requires significant organizational changes, including crossfunctional collaboration, new capabilities in data literacy and algorithmic thinking, and the emergence of hybrid roles that integrate marketing and technology expertise. Human implications are equally profound, as routine tasks become automated and marketers assume roles emphasizing creativity, strategy, and ethical judgment, raising concerns about skill displacement and workforce polarization. Additionally, marketing automation introduces ethical, social, and governance challenges, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, and accountability. Firms must balance innovation with transparency, trust, and responsible use of AI to maintain customer confidence. This study highlights the multidimensional impact of marketing automation, emphasizing the need for integrated research that considers strategic, organizational, human, and ethical perspectives in shaping its future trajectory.

detail.title: The Impact of Participation and Resource Allocation on Economic Empowerment of Communities through the Bendosari Edu-Tourism Program
detail.abstract: This paper explores the subject of rural economic empowerment by examining the Bendosari edu-tourism project of Sleman, Yogyakarta, Indonesia. The paper targets three levers which often define the occurrence of sustainable local benefits of community-based tourism namely community participation, strategic resource allocation, and the collaboration of stakeholders. A mixed-method research design was used. The quantitative information was collected using a structured questionnaire that was distributed among 100 study participants chosen with the help of the stratified random sampling; the qualitative data was collected with the help of interviews with members of the local community and focus group discussions. The multiple linear regression outcomes suggest that the strongest positive impact on the economic empowerment is played by participation (β = 0.45, p < 0.001), then there is resource allocation (β = 0.38, p = 0.001) and stakeholder collaboration (β = 0.29, p = 0.004). The overall model is statistically significant (F = 25.67, p < 0.001) and explains 61% of the variance in economic empowerment (R² = 0.61; Adjusted R² = 0.59). Qualitative findings help explain the “how” behind these coefficients: participation increases perceived ownership and responsibility, resource support reduces production and market frictions, and collaboration improves coordination, access, and problem solving. The paper adds a reviewer-safe, empirically based explanation of how bundled interventions on edutourism can enhance the livelihoods of the rural population without contravening the ideals of sustainability. The policy implications give more focus to institutionalized participation, selective investment in productive assets and marketing power, and sustainable multi-actor relations in governance.

detail.abstract: Over the past two decades, digital technologies have profoundly reshaped marketing and consumer behavior, giving rise to neuromarketing, an interdisciplinary field integrating neuroscience, psychology, and marketing science. Neuromarketing examines the subconscious neural mechanisms underlying perception, emotion, and decision-making, offering insights beyond traditional self-reports. Contemporary research demonstrates that many consumer choices are automatic, emotional, and heuristic-driven, with dual-process cognition highlighting the dominance of intuitive, fast, and affective systems in everyday purchases. Artificial intelligence (AI) amplifies these mechanisms by delivering real-time, hyper-personalized content through recommendation engines, dynamic pricing, affective computing, and conversational agents. AI-driven platforms engineer environments that optimize attention, reward anticipation, and emotional vulnerability, systematically facilitating impulsive and emotionally charged consumption. Neuroimaging and physiological measures reveal the neural correlates of these behaviors, including heightened activity in reward circuits and attenuated self-regulatory control. Despite its practical potential, the integration of AI with neuromarketing raises ethical concerns regarding consumer autonomy, informed consent, psychological exploitation, and algorithmic bias. This study provides a comprehensive theoretical synthesis of AI-enhanced neuromarketing, elucidates the cognitive and behavioral mechanisms of impulsive consumption, and highlights the normative and regulatory implications necessary for responsible application. Future research should address longitudinal, cross-cultural, and ethical dimensions to balance commercial efficacy with consumer welfare.

detail.abstract:
Conventional policy and sustainability frameworks often assume that human behavior can be reshaped through moral persuasion, regulatory enforcement, or normative incentives. However, repeated failures in climate policy, environmental regulation, and ESG finance reveal a deeper structural limitation: human self-interest is treated as an external disturbance rather than a core design variable.

This paper introduces Meatball Theory, a behavioral–structural framework grounded in Behavior-Aligned System Design (BASD). The theory reconceptualizes human self-interest not as a flaw to be corrected, but as a neutral and predictable behavioral constant that must be embedded within system architecture. Using the metaphor of a child who resists vegetables but willingly consumes them when embedded within a meatball, the paper illustrates how desired outcomes can be achieved without requiring changes in intrinsic preferences or moral alignment.

The paper advances three core arguments. First, purity-based designs that rely on ethical intention, voluntary compliance, or transparent moral signaling systematically fail under economic and behavioral constraints. Second, increasing socially desirable components does not necessarily raise total system cost; rather, resistance arises from transition friction and preference inertia, which are frequently misinterpreted as economic infeasibility. Third, transparency imposed at the execution stage often induces behavioral reversal, whereas transparency applied at the outcome-verification stage strengthens accountability without distorting choice.

By reframing externalities as internal design parameters and positioning finance as a structural binder rather than a moral lever, Meatball Theory provides a pragmatic foundation for climate systems, sustainable finance, and institutional design. The framework explains why behavior-aligned systems outperform virtue-based interventions and offers a replicable logic for constructing systems that work with human nature rather than against it.

detail.abstract: The healthcare industry is currently facing a "Pilot Purgatory" crisis, where approximately 90% of Artificial Intelligence (AI) projects fail to scale beyond the initial pilot phase. This perspective paper introduces the "Greenhouse Fallacy" as a primary framework for understanding this failure rate. detail.title: Under what Institutional and Incentive Conditions do Skill-Development Subsidies Outperform Direct Wage Support in Improving Long-Term Labour Market Outcomes in India?
detail.abstract: Governments seeking to raise labour productivity face a persistent policy dilemma between providing direct wage support and subsidising skill development. While wage support can stabilise incomes and boost labour supply in the short term, skill-development subsidies are often promoted as a means of enhancing long-term employability and productivity, though their effectiveness varies widely across contexts. This paper asks: under what institutional and incentive conditions do skill-development subsidies outperform direct wage support in improving long-term labour market outcomes? Using a comparative policy analysis based on secondary data from OECD, World Bank, and ILO evaluations, the paper examines how labour market incentives, employer participation, and institutional capacity shape policy performance. The analysis finds that skill-development subsidies generate superior long-term outcomes when programs are closely aligned with labour market demand, supported by credible employer involvement, and implemented by institutions capable of enforcing targeting and quality standards. In the absence of these conditions, direct wage support often delivers more predictable short-to medium-term results. The paper contributes to the labour economics literature by emphasising the conditional nature of policy effectiveness and by identifying design principles for integrating income support with human capital investment.

title: Access to Justice from a Preventive Perspective in Civil Law Systems

detail.title: Access to Justice from a Preventive Perspective in Civil Law Systems
detail.abstract:
Access to justice has traditionally been understood as access to courts and judicial remedies. While judicial protection remains an essential guarantee of the rule of law, this article argues that a purely jurisdictional conception of access to justice is insufficient to ensure the effective and equal protection of rights in contemporary societies. Drawing on the civil law tradition, the paper develops a preventive and institutional approach to access to justice, emphasizing the role of public legal institutions endowed with public faith (fe pública).

The article analyses the notarial function and civil registration systems as core institutions of preventive justice. It argues that notaries and civil registrars operate ex ante, ensuring legality, legal certainty, and the official recognition of personal legal status before conflicts arise. By producing public documents and exercising preventive legality control, these institutions reduce litigation, protect vulnerable individuals, and strengthen institutional trust. Through a comparative perspective focused on Spain and Italy, the paper demonstrates that preventive justice constitutes a structural feature of civil law systems and a necessary dimension of effective access to justice.

title: The Job Characteristics Model in the Age of Large Language Models: A Multi-Architecture Analysis of AI-Augmented Work Design

detail.title: The Job Characteristics Model in the Age of Large Language Models: A Multi-Architecture Analysis of AI-Augmented Work Design
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming knowledge work, yet their implications for fundamental work design theory remain underexplored. This study examines how LLM integration affects the Job Characteristics Model (JCM), a foundational framework linking work design to employee outcomes. Using hierarchical linear modeling with a comprehensive simulated dataset (N = 10,000 knowledge workers across 30 organizational contexts), we analyze five major LLM architectures (GPT-4o, o1-preview, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and openweight models) under varying implementation conditions. Results demonstrate that LLM augmentation substantially enhances core job characteristics-particularly skill variety (+0.95 SD on average, ranging to +1.15 SD for multimodal architectures), task significance (+0.63 SD), and feedback quality (+0.71 SD)-with architecture-specific patterns emerging based on reasoning capabilities, multimodal integration, and customization options. The motivating potential score (MPS) increased by approximately 61% on average (from baseline M=106 to M=170), with effects moderated by growth need strength (GNS), override authority levels, and advanced AI features. Multi-architecture portfolios achieved 23% higher MPS gains than single-architecture implementations (η² = 0.19, p < 0.001) but required 127% greater implementation investment. Trajectory analyses revealed sustained improvements over 24 months, with high-GNS workers showing accelerating benefits while low-GNS workers plateaued after 12 months. These findings suggest LLMs can fundamentally enrich work design when thoughtfully implemented, though benefits depend critically on architecture selection, worker characteristics, and organizational support structures. We propose an expanded theoretical framework integrating AI capabilities into JCM constructs and discuss implications for human-AI work design.

detail.abstract: Trade and investment promotion organizations (TPOs) are undergoing rapid digital and managerial modernization, incorporating CRM systems, pipeline dashboards, and increasingly AI-enabled analytics to respond to expanding mandates and growing accountability pressures. However, this paper argues that the central challenge facing public economic promotion is not the adoption of such tools, but their frequent misordering in the absence of a coherent institutional architecture. When privatesector conversion logics and purchase funnels implicitly structure public action, promotion agencies drift toward transactional proxies and short-term verification, undermining firm capability development and long-term policy effectiveness. The paper advances a normative framework grounded in public value creation and firm capability development, aligned with World Bank, United Nations, and ECLAC perspectives. It makes three core contributions. First, it reasserts domestic firms as the primary subjects of public promotion policy, while situating international buyers and investors as essential market actors rather than policy beneficiaries. Second, it distinguishes flywheels as accumulative, non-teleological institutional architectures from funnels as sequencing devices, arguing that the only legitimate policy-level funnel is an outbound capability funnel oriented toward firm graduation and autonomous internationalization. Third, it reconceptualizes CRM systems as public relational infrastructure-memory and learning systems that support institutional continuity rather than decision or sales frameworks. By reordering tools, actors, and objectives, the paper offers a policy-consistent approach to modernization with direct implications for governance, metrics, and the responsible deployment of AI in trade and investment promotion agencies operating under multilateral accountability standards.

Motivated by geopolitical vulnerabilities exposing the Philippines' dependence on foreign defense suppliers and the recent enactment of the SRDP Revitalization Act (RA 12024), this study analyzes current national policies and foreign defense innovation models to identify gaps in the utilization of the reserve force. title: A vision-based deep reinforcement learning control of windows and thermostats in naturally-ventilated building for environment management and energy conservation

detail.title: A vision-based deep reinforcement learning control of windows and thermostats in naturally-ventilated building for environment management and energy conservation
detail.abstract: Occupant behavior (OB) has been shown to strongly affect building energy performance. In recent years, computer vision (CV) and occupant-centric control (OCC) have been widely used to improve the operation of mechanical ventilation systems. However, their use in managing natural ventilation, especially in resolving the wintertime conflict between maintaining indoor air quality (from window opening) and minimizing heating demand, remains a notable research gap. To address this, we developed and evaluated a novel OCC strategy that coordinated thermostats with window operation. The strategy closed the loop between real-time occupant sensing, data-driven decision-making, and actuation of building systems. The strategy leveraged real-time OB data obtained from CV-aided cameras (occupant presence, count, activity, window status) over a four-day period, and was implemented within a Python-EnergyPlus co-simulation platform for training. The core of the strategy was a Deep Q-Network (DQN) controller that dynamically adjusted window openings, coupled with an occupancy-driven heating switch. Simulation results showed that, compared to baseline cases using scheduled heating and real-time window opening profile, our approach could reduce heating demand by 60.5%-64.3%, improved the mean Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) by 0.85 to 1.89 (65.8–81.1% enhancement respectively), and consistently maintained CO₂ concentrations below 1000 ppm. This work demonstrated the feasibility and significant benefits of vision-guided deep reinforcement learning for integrated natural ventilation and heating control in cold climates.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This paper introduces the From Kenya With Care (FKWC) framework and its Communication Readiness System (CRS), designed to operationalize narrative economics at the cooperative level and enable smallholder farmers to capture greater value through ethical storytelling. title: Adaptive AI Governance: A Common Temporal Frame for Constructive Autonomy

detail.title: Adaptive AI Governance: A Common Temporal Frame for Constructive Autonomy
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence has shifted organisational decision-making from episodic judgment to continuous execution. Across functions, sectors, and institutions, systems now act, learn, and adapt at speeds that exceed the cadence of human oversight and formal governance. This working paper introduces a common frame for AI governance grounded not in controls, policies, or dashboards, but in temporal design.

The frame addresses a recurring structural condition—authority lag—in which execution becomes continuous while authority remains periodic. Building on traditions in organization design, cybernetics, and systems governance, the paper proposes a universal architectural pattern composed of dual operational loops, a cadence bridge, and a structural evolution layer. This architecture is function-agnostic by design, allowing it to be instantiated differently across domains while preserving a shared logic of legitimacy, adaptability, and trust.

Rather than offering a prescriptive governance model or implementation methodology, the paper provides a descriptive architectural frame—a way of seeing how automation, human judgment, and institutional authority must be arranged in time if AI-enabled organisations are to remain both effective and governable. The frame is intended to support further research, teaching, and applied design work, and may evolve through continued use and refinement.

detail.title: Research on Risk Dependency Structures and Resource Allocation Optimization in New Energy Technology Collaboration within Enterprise Distributed Innovation
detail.abstract: As new energy technology systems grow increasingly complex, corporate innovation activities in photovoltaics, energy storage, wind power, and energy management exhibit distinct distributed characteristics. Cross-enterprise collaboration and cross-regional innovation have become pivotal drivers for industrial upgrading. However, the lengthy new energy industrial chain, numerous participants, and high technical coupling lead to significant knowledge stickiness in knowledge transfer processes, thereby impairing collaborative innovation efficiency.To address this issue, this paper constructs a probabilistic resource allocation optimization model for distributed innovation networks in new energy enterprises. First, Least Squares Support Vector Machine (LSSVM) is employed to predict the success rate of collaborative innovation tasks. Model parameters are jointly optimized using grid search and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) under RBF, Polynomial, and Sigmoid kernel functions to adapt to different types of technological coupling and knowledge stickiness structures.Subsequently, a Gaussian Copula is introduced to characterize the risk dependency structure among technological maturity, external market volatility, and R&D collaboration complexity between innovation nodes. This enables the calculation of conditional value at risk (CoVaR) to quantify collaborative innovation risks under high uncertainty in new energy technologies. During resource allocation, a cost-loss model based on Bayesian decision theory is established, and the simulated annealing algorithm is employed to solve for the optimal combination of R&D and collaborative resources.Simulation results demonstrate that under conditions of rapid new energy technology iteration and significant knowledge stickiness, this method reduces resource waste by 17%-23% compared to traditional empirical allocation approaches while enhancing cross-enterprise innovation collaboration efficiency. This study provides a quantifiable and interpretable decision-making method for distributed innovation management in the new energy industry, holding significant implications for building an efficient industrial collaborative innovation ecosystem.

title: Optimizing Gated Content Strategy Through Visitor Personas in B2B Marketing

detail.title: Optimizing Gated Content Strategy Through Visitor Personas in B2B Marketing

detail.abstract: Gated content is widely used in business-to-business (B2B) digital marketing to convert anonymous website visitors into identifiable leads, yet its effectiveness remains contested due to the trade-off between lead capture and audience reach. Prior research has largely evaluated gated content using binary conversion metrics, offering limited insight into how heterogeneous visitor engagement behaviors shape downstream purchase intent. Drawing on engagement theory, this study examines gated content performance through an engagement-state lens. Using large-scale behavioral data from a B2B technology firm (approximately 215,000 visitors over an eight-month period), we identify three distinct engagement states based on observable behaviors: Responders (form submitters), Engagers (meaningful interaction without submission), and Bouncers (minimal interaction). We evaluate downstream purchase intent using a longitudinal behavioral proxy-subsequent visits to high-intent pages within a 90-day window. The findings show that while form submission is a strong indicator of buyer readiness, it captures only a subset of total demand influenced by gated content. A non-trivial proportion of Engagers later exhibit high-intent behavior, indicating that engagement without disclosure represents latent demand overlooked by conversion-only metrics. Asset-level value and device context further moderate the effectiveness of gating, with mobile interaction amplifying disclosure friction. This study contributes to marketing analytics and digital marketing literature by reframing gated content effectiveness through engagement-state heterogeneity and by extending measurement beyond immediate conversion events. The results offer both theoretical insight into non-linear B2B customer journeys and practical guidance for designing selective, context-aware gated content strategies.

title: The Naked Truth from the Single Stock Futures Market
affiliations: New York University, Leonard N. Stern School of Business and Southern Methodist University (SMU) - Finance Department

detail.title: The Naked Truth from the Single Stock Futures Market
detail.abstract: In this paper, we use a novel high-frequency data set, provided by the OneChicago single stock futures exchange, to study the impact of short sale restrictions on asset prices. Contrary to Battalio and Scultz (2006), we find many violations to the put call parity relation and to the cost of carry model even when using perfectly synchronous futures and stock prices. Most of these violations occur in a direction consistent with stocks being short-sale constrained. Examining the future put call parity relation that involves no equity, we find that futures and options are fairly priced, relative to each other. Constructing an implied intra-day measure of stock's short-sale rebate rate from stock and futures prices, we show that, contrary to many critics' claims, the SEC's ban of naked short selling on 19 financial stocks in July 2008 was highly effective in raising the overall cost of shorting. After remaining at the zero level for a week, on the first day the ban was effective, the average implied short sale rebate rate on the 19 financial firms instantly dropped to -4% p.a. and eventually -8% p.a. within a couple of days.

detail.abstract: Disasters, like pandemics and earthquakes and floods and hurricanes really mess up peoples lives and how businesses work. These things make people very unsure and scared. They think they will not have enough of what they need. So people do things differently than they normally do. When something bad happens people often buy a lot of things at once they store up food and water and other important things they make purchases without thinking. They use the internet to shop more. At the time companies have a lot of trouble keeping up with getting products to people making sure they have enough of what people want being fair and making sure people still trust them. This paper is about how people buy things when bad things happen, like disasters. It looks at what businesses do to deal with the changes in the way people buy things during these times. The paper uses information from studies around the world and from Sri Lanka to show what affects how people buy things like how they feel what others think and what is happening around them. It also looks at what businesses do like being fair, with prices talking to people during a crisis changing how they get things to people and using things. The study helps us understand what happens when disasters occur and how businesses and people who make rules can work together. It looks at what we know and finds the missing pieces to help businesses and policymakers make good decisions during disasters and crises especially when it comes to consumer behaviour and marketing strategies.

title: Firm-Level Technology Adoption in Times of Crisis

detail.title: Firm-Level Technology Adoption in Times of Crisis
detail.abstract: We investigate the diffusion of frontier technologies across German firms before and during the Covid-19 crisis. Our analysis tracks the nature, timing, and pandemic-related motivations behind technology investments, using tailor-made longitudinal survey data linked to administrative worker–firm records. Technologies adopted after the onset of the pandemic increasingly facilitated remote work and mitigated the negative employment effects of the crisis. Overall, however, investments in frontier technologies declined sharply, equivalent to a loss of 1.4 years of pre-pandemic investment activity. This procyclical adoption pattern is particularly striking since the pandemic created clear incentives to experiment with new technologies. Our findings highlight how short-run fluctuations may influence mediumrun economic growth through their impact on technology diffusion.

title: In Faith We Create: Political Ideology, Religion, and Corporate Risk-taking
affiliations: Nanjing Audit University and Huazhong University of Science and Technology - School of Economics

detail.title: In Faith We Create: Political Ideology, Religion, and Corporate Risk-taking
detail.abstract: How faith -- either political ideology or religion  -- impact entrepreneurs' innovation behavior? Using the 2018Enterprise Survey for Innovation and Entrepreneurship (ESIEC), with 58,500 small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in China, we find that religious entrepreneurs exhibit a higher tendency to try riskier innovation and higher innovation expenditures. Although for firms managed by members of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), we find little evidence for the extensive margins of innovation participation; we observe a significant increase in the intensive margins. Active participation in innovation among religious entrepreneurs can be explained by their higher confidence and commitment level in investment in R\&D, as well as their greater access to government financial support. A further analysis of the unexpected outbreak of COVID-19 reveals that innovative firms with faith outperformed their counterparts at the beginning of the pandemic. This suggests that faithful managers tend to be more far-sighted and efficient in allocating corporate resources when they experience an unexpected downturn.

title: When Sustainability Support Falls Flat: How Manufacturer's Double-Agency Role Shapes Effort in Multi-Tier Supply Chains
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen - School of Management and Economics and Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University

detail.title: When Sustainability Support Falls Flat: How Manufacturer's Double-Agency Role Shapes Effort in Multi-Tier Supply Chains
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Sustainability violations at upstream suppliers expose downstream supply chain members to reputational and financial risks, yet retailers struggle to induce adequate sustainability effort in multi-tier supply chains. We study the strategic role of a mid-tier manufacturer that faces a double-agency problem. The manufacturer must balance its own sustainability effort to minimize the loss faced by the retailer and itself, while relying on an upstream supplier whose incentives to invest in sustainability are weaker. Methodology/results: We develop a three-tier game-theoretic model in which violation risk depends on supplier and manufacturer efforts, and the manufacturer also sets a support level to facilitate supplier investment. Under risk-neutral rationality, penalty versus bonus framing and simultaneous versus delayed manufacturer effort choices are payoff-equivalent and yield the same equilibrium benchmarks. We compare two decision sequences for the manufacturer (simultaneous versus delayed effort choice) and two contract frames (penalty versus bonus) that are normatively equivalent under risk neutrality and derive benchmarks. We then test this setting in two pre-registered laboratory experiments. Across both studies, manufacturer effort is close to the normative benchmark, but support is systematically underprovided and suppliers substantially underinvest and respond weakly to support, leading to total sustainability effort and supply chain profits below theoretical predictions. Contract framing has little impact on behavior, whereas requiring the manufacturer to commit its own effort simultaneously with support generates higher total sustainability effort than allowing delayed effort choices. Managerial implications: Our results suggest that the primary bottleneck in multi-tier sustainability is manufacturer reluctance to assist and limited supplier responsiveness to manufacturer’s assistance, and that mechanisms which enhance supplier incentives and promote early manufacturer commitment are more effective than re-framing contracts or increasing pressure on intermediaries.

title: Optimizing Daily Max Estimation in University Powerlifting: A Machine Learning Approach to RPE-Velocity Correlation

detail.abstract: Traditional periodization models often fail to account for the daily fluctuations in an athlete's physiological state, particularly in the collegiate environment where academic stress and sleep irregularity are prevalent. This paper proposes a localized machine learning framework to refine autoregulation in powerlifting. By analyzing the correlation between subjective Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) and objective mean concentric velocity (MCV) during the back squat, I developed a predictive model to estimate daily 1RM (One-Repetition Maximum). Data collected from a sample of collegiate lifters via smartphone-based computer vision tracking suggests that an integrated AI-driven feedback loop provides more accurate daily load adjustments than traditional RPE-only methods, reducing the risk of overreaching while optimizing strength acquisition.

title: Convexity of Inverse Blocking Curves in Loss Systems

detail.abstract: We study the inverse of the Erlang loss (Erlang-B) formula, namely the maximum offered load supportable at a fixed blocking target as a function of the number of servers. We show that this inverse blocking curve is strictly increasing and globally convex, yielding an exact economies-of-scale statement for loss-system dimensioning. The proof is based on a tilted-measure representation and extends to the finite-waiting-room multi-server model.

title: Why Governments Keep Missing Technology Crises Before They Happen: From WannaCry to AI
affiliations: University of Liverpool

detail.title: Why Governments Keep Missing Technology Crises Before They Happen: From WannaCry to AI
detail.abstract: Parliamentary inquiries following the WannaCry ransomware attack revealed a disturbing pattern: government institutions had complied with security standards yet remained catastrophically vulnerable. The problem lies not in implementation failures but in the structure of democratic oversight. Technology oversight operates on annual planning cycles while threats evolve monthly, creating systematic blind spots that turn compliance into false confidence. Rather than reflecting individual or organisational shortcomings, this pattern arises from governance architectures calibrated for slower technological eras. As the UK builds regulatory frameworks for artificial intelligence, it risks embedding these structural failures into systems where consequences will be far more severe. This article proposes three institutional reforms, grounded in parliamentary evidence and comparative governance analysis: continuous reassessment with flow-constrained prioritisation, a real-time intelligence infrastructure as a public good, and regulatory frameworks designed to trigger their own revision. These mechanisms address governance temporality as the core failure mode in technology oversight.

title: Demand-Driven Contractual Closed-Loop Theory : A Framework for Resource Allocation Based on Real Usage Feedback

detail.title: Demand-Driven Contractual Closed-Loop Theory : A Framework for Resource Allocation Based on Real Usage Feedback
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a new institutional and resource allocation framework, termed Demand-Driven Contractual Closed-Loop Theory (DDCCLT). The theory addresses the structural limitations of traditional allocation mechanisms-such as price signals, administrative planning, and prediction-based models-under conditions of high automation, digitalization, and platform-based coordination. Rather than relying on ex ante forecasts, statistical demand estimation, or centralized decision-making, DDCCLT emphasizes "real usage behavior" as a continuous feedback signal for contract execution, resource reallocation, and institutional adjustment. By structuring resource allocation as a recursive closed loop-Demand → Contract → Execution → Feedback → Re-contracting-the framework illustrates how dynamic coordination can emerge without centralized prediction. By internalizing usage feedback as a generative institutional mechanism, DDCCLT offers a pathway to minimize allocative inefficiencies caused by speculative pricing and rigid planning models. The contribution of this paper is conceptual and structural. It introduces a general theoretical framework intended to serve as a foundation for future formal modeling, empirical simulation, and applied research in algorithmic governance.

detail.abstract: AI is compressing competitive time by reducing the cost of execution across design, development, coordination, and deployment. As a result, many downstream advantages become less durable, leadership turns over more quickly, and discretionary stock picking becomes harder. The same dynamic creates a design problem for passive investors: low-cost index implementation relies on rules that constrain turnover and trading frictions, even as categories and winners can change faster. This paper offers a practitioner framework in three steps. First, it argues that scarcity persists and relocates upstream into bottlenecks that are difficult to scale quickly, including compute supply chains, grid capacity and interconnection, and trusted data and institutions. Second, it treats passive as a design space and identifies index methodology levers that improve representational responsiveness subject to a turnover budget. Third, it proposes a rotation-survival portfolio that combines a broad-market anchor, diversified bottleneck sleeves with broad inclusion, and modest rules-based guardrails to remain invested through scarcity rotation rather than time it.

title: A Predictive Framework for Dynamic Stakeholder Management in Volatile Environments

detail.title: A Predictive Framework for Dynamic Stakeholder Management in Volatile Environments
detail.abstract: Contemporary organisational environments are characterised by rapid and non-linear shifts in stakeholder alignment driven by geopolitical change, regulatory evolution, technological disruption, and value reconfiguration. This paper introduces the Predictive Stakeholder Positioning Model, a framework that extends classical stakeholder theory by incorporating stakeholder propensity as a predictive dimension alongside conventional measures of power, interest, and engagement. Drawing on dynamic stakeholder literature, behavioural stakeholder research, and longitudinal organisational observation, the model conceptualises propensity as a latent dispositional inclination that is temporally prior to observable engagement. By identifying shifts in propensity before they materialise into overt support or opposition, leaders gain strategic opportunities for anticipatory relationship management. The framework has been operationalised in a digital stakeholder-management platform enabling temporal tracking, network visualisation and scenario planning.

title: Comprehensive Analysis of Shared E-Scooter Micromobility Services in Turin, Italy

detail.title: Comprehensive Analysis of Shared E-Scooter Micromobility Services in Turin, Italy
detail.abstract: This report presents an empirical analysis of shared electric scooter (e-scooter) operations in Turin, Italy. We examine 2,548,650 validated trips from three licensed operators (LIME, VOI, and BIRD) spanning a 23-month observation period (January 2024 to November 2025). The analysis addresses five key research questions: (1) data quality and temporal mobility patterns, (2) origin-destination flow structures using Turin's official statistical zones, (3) competition versus complementarity with public transport, (4) parking duration patterns and ghost vehicle identification, and (5) economic feasibility through profit-and-loss analysis. Our findings reveal that e-scooters function primarily as first-mile/last-mile connectors, with a 95.1% feeder rate at the 200-meter buffer threshold, rather than direct competitors to public transport. Parking analysis identified only 0.15% ghost vehicles (parked more than 120 hours), indicating efficient fleet utilization. The combined market generates €8.30 million annually with a 57.7% profit margin, indicating strong financial sustainability without need for municipal subsidies.

title: A Taxonomy of AI Governance Approaches: Distinguishing Visibility, Alignment, and Authorization

The concepts and definitions presented in this paper were developed independently as a theoretical and technical taxonomy and are published for general scholarly and evaluative use. detail.abstract:
The term AI governance is increasingly applied to a wide range of practices, including logging, monitoring, model alignment, guardrails, and policy documentation. This conceptual overloading obscures a critical distinction: many widely deployed “governance” mechanisms provide visibility into system behavior or influence model outputs, but do not establish whether a specific AI-mediated action was authorized under binding policy constraints at the time of execution.

This paper proposes a taxonomy that separates AI governance into three fundamentally different problem domains: operational visibility, behavioral alignment, and decision authorization. It argues that authorization constitutes a distinct governance function that cannot be satisfied by post-hoc audit logs, probabilistic alignment techniques, or policy workflows alone. The paper introduces a formal, falsifiable definition of deterministic AI governance, defined as a pre-execution authorization layer in which identical governed state produces identical governance verdicts and where systems emit replayable, verifier-grade decision artifacts sufficient for independent third-party verification.

The taxonomy specifies the minimum requirements for such governance, including a normative definition of governed state, a minimum evidence package, an enforcement triad (ALLOW / DENY / ABSTAIN) with fail-closed semantics, and a set of adversarial “anti-laundering” tests designed to distinguish genuine governance from trust-based or vendor-dependent imitations. The paper is intended to provide enterprise buyers, regulators, auditors, and researchers with a shared vocabulary and concrete evaluation criteria for assessing AI governance claims in high-stakes, regulated environments.

detail.title: Legal Order in the Age of AI Agents

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Toronto Law Journal (forthcoming, 2026)

detail.abstract: As AI tools increasingly shape everyday life, autonomous AI agents are emerging as a new frontier. This Article demonstrates how AI legal agents, empowered to act independently on behalf of human users, could structurally reconfigure legal systems through three transformative pathways. First, AI legal agents promise to democratize legal knowledge by dismantling vertical and horizontal institutional barriers to justice. Second, these agents could reconstitute legal authority through algorithmic constitutionalism, accelerated jurisdictional synthesis, and legal pluralism, enabling novel frameworks of AI-mediated dispute resolution that challenge traditional paradigms of jurisdiction and legitimacy. Third, such agents may shift the temporal focus of legal intervention from post-violation remediation to continuous preventive measures. Harnessing this triple transformation-the democratization, pluralistic reconstitution, and temporal shift-will require design frameworks that balance accountability with efficiency, fairness with personalization, and societal values with algorithmic optimization. Together, these developments gesture toward a legal singularity, a future in which AI legal agents, through their continuous interaction with human judgment and institutional frameworks, render law increasingly self-organizing, adaptive, and intelligible.

title: Market Return Decomposition and Equity Risk Premium Predictability

detail.title: Market Return Decomposition and Equity Risk Premium Predictability
detail.abstract: We introduce a novel decomposition of stock market returns into a fundamental component (FC), capturing long-term growth, and an unexpected capital gain component (UC), reflecting short-term fluctuations. The FC aligns with highly persistent valuation ratios, while the UC is predictable via standard regressions, further improved by shrinkage. Using 41 predictors from Goyal et al. We argue that predictors jointly contain valuable information about stock returns, with combination forecasts showing significant out-of-sample predictive power, reaffirming the predictability of the equity risk premium documented in prior research.

title: Making Employers: The Effects of Supporting First Hires in a Large-Scale Randomized Experiment

detail.title: Making Employers: The Effects of Supporting First Hires in a Large-Scale Randomized Experiment
detail.abstract: Most entrepreneurs operate without employees. Hiring may be unprofitable for them, but they may also be reluctant to pay the one-time costs of becoming an employer due to attentional costs, risk aversion, or credit constraints. We examine the extent to which a temporary subsidy to hire first employees induces entrepreneurs to become employers in a large-scale randomized experiment. The experiment offered to 34,500 randomly selected non-employer entrepreneurs e 10,000 to cover 50% of the wage costs of first employees. We find a 20% increase in the fraction of firms that hire workers, with effects of similar magnitude on wage costs and number of employees. The effects stay positive at 7% after the subsidy period, indicating that the temporary subsidy created new permanent employers. Our results suggest that frictions in hiring first employees can be an important barrier for employer entry and firm growth.

title: Autonomous Weapon Systems and AI-Enabled Decision Support Systems in Military Targeting: A Comparison and Recommended Policy Responses

detail.title: Autonomous Weapon Systems and AI-Enabled Decision Support Systems in Military Targeting: A Comparison and Recommended Policy Responses
detail.abstract: This report provides a comparative analysis of autonomous weapon systems (AWS) and artificial intelligence-enabled decision support systems (AI-DSS) used in in military targeting. It examines how both technologies shape human roles in decision making about the use of force, assesses their respective risks of unintended harm and analyses the key issues they raise under international law. By mapping the key similarities and differences between AWS and AI-DSS—particularly in their deployment across different phases of the targeting cycle—the report clarifies where existing policy frameworks apply and where gaps remain. It outlines three options for policymakers with regards to AI-DSS: integrate AI-DSS into current AWS processes, establish a dedicated track for AI-DSS or pursue no targeted response. The report concludes with three actionable recommendations aimed at supporting responsible governance: explore the need for a separate multilateral process for AI-DSS, build on lessons from AWS governance and prioritize research to guide the responsible integration of AI into military decision making.
