declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interests to be declared by the authors.

detail.abstract: Organised crime infiltration into public administrations represents a critical threat to democratic governance and effective local service delivery. In Italy, municipal council dissolutions are the most robust legal indicator of such infiltration, yet they remain a reactive measure. This study investigates whether socioeconomic and administrative conditions can signal an elevated risk of mafia-related infiltration prior to institutional breakdown. Leveraging publicly available socio-demographic municipal data from the Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT), we develop a machine learning pipeline capable of predicting dissolution events up to two years in advance. The model, based on logistic regression with Weight of Evidence transformation and stepwise variable selection, achieves significant discriminative power (ROC AUC = 0.78 on the test set) while maintaining full interpretability. To overcome the limitations of numerical outputs in decision-making contexts, we introduce a post-hoc explainability layer that leverages SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) values to trace the statistical contribution of each variable. These outputs are then translated into structured, human-readable narrative reports through a Large Language Model (LLM), enabling a more accessible and transparent understanding of municipal risk profiles. This hybrid architecture provides a scalable and operationally viable tool for early risk detection and strategic decision support in crime prevention.

title: The Austrian Case against Capitalism
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Austrian Case against Capitalism
detail.abstract: The Austrian School of Economics is widely regarded as a prime exponent of the capitalist system. It is thus highly ironic that its core defense of capitalism-namely, Mises' famous calculation argument-is fundamentally neoclassical in nature. Due to inconsistencies in Mises' thought, the Austrian conception of capitalism is flawed. Mises rejected the idea of money-as-aveil in his monetary thought but reintroduced this concept in his explication of the market pricing process for consumer and producer goods (culminating in his idea of consumer sovereignty). Mises' regression theorem conflicts with his calculation argument. As well, Austrian economics views capitalism as simply an advanced market system and is thus historically inaccurate. I will argue here that the Marxian description of capitalism is, to a large degree, correct, and that certain insights can be incorporated into Austrian analysis.

title: Generalised Cost Analysis of Urban Mobility Options: A Comparative Study of Transport Modes

detail.title: Generalised Cost Analysis of Urban Mobility Options: A Comparative Study of Transport Modes
detail.abstract: This report presents a comprehensive analysis of generalised cost (C g) for thirteen urban mobility options available for a home-university commute in Turin, Italy. The study evaluates both private and shared transport modes by quantifying monetary expenditures and the economic value of travel time. Using a base case Value of Time (VOT) of 10 EUR per hour, we calculate annual generalised costs ranging from EUR 1,249 (Private E-Scooter) to EUR 9,031 (Uber). The analysis includes sensitivity testing across VOT values from 8 to 200 EUR per hour, revealing that optimal mode choice depends significantly on individual time valuation. Results demonstrate that personal micro-mobility options provide the lowest generalised costs for typical commuters, while traditional private car ownership ranks among the most expensive options due to substantial parking costs that represent 56% of total financial expenditures. The findings provide practical guidance for commuters and urban planners seeking to optimize transport choices based on total economic cost rather than monetary cost alone.

title: Trump's Venezuela Intervention: A Critical Assessment of Geopolitical Strategy and Global Financial Market Ramifications

detail.title: Trump's Venezuela Intervention: A Critical Assessment of Geopolitical Strategy and Global Financial Market Ramifications
detail.abstract: President Donald Trump's military intervention in Venezuela on January 3, 2026, resulting in President Nicolás Maduro's capture, represents an unprecedented escalation in U.S. foreign policy with profound implications for global financial markets. This qualitative case study examines multidimensional impacts across oil markets, sovereign debt, currency dynamics, and geopolitical alignments. Findings reveal paradoxical market responses: immediate stability masking structural uncertainties. Oil prices remained subdued due to Venezuela's diminished production and global oversupply, while defense and energy equities surged on reconstruction expectations. Venezuelan bonds experienced speculative rallies despite questionable fundamentals. The intervention accelerated China's energy vulnerabilities, undermined international legal norms, and created precedents that may embolden rival powers, fundamentally challenging dollar hegemony and market-based political risk assessments.

detail.title: Quantum Security Risks and the Decentralization Paradox of Bitcoin

detail.abstract:
Recent advances in quantum computing have renewed concerns about the long-term security of Bitcoin and other cryptographic assets. Existing discussions largely frame quantum security risks as purely technical threats that could undermine cryptographic primitives and destabilize the network. This paper argues that such a perspective is incomplete.

Rather than treating quantum risk solely as an exogenous technological shock, this study conceptualizes it as a structural variable that may interact asymmetrically with Bitcoin’s ownership distribution and governance dynamics. In particular, Bitcoin holdings associated with early address types and long-dormant wallets—where public keys are persistently exposed or where proactive migration is infeasible—may face structurally higher vulnerability under plausible quantum attack scenarios.

Using a conditional and non-predictive analytical framework, this paper does not attempt to forecast the timing or feasibility of quantum attacks. Instead, it examines how the perception and selective impact of quantum security risk could induce shifts in asset mobility, ownership concentration, and governance incentives within the Bitcoin network.

The analysis suggests that quantum security risk embodies a decentralization paradox: it may simultaneously enable greater dispersion of ownership through forced liquidity while also accelerating recentralization if vulnerable assets are absorbed by capital-intensive actors. This structural perspective highlights quantum risk not as a deterministic threat to Bitcoin’s survival, but as a potential catalyst for endogenous transformation in its economic and governance structure.

detail.title: Econometric Analysis of Crude Oil Price Dynamics using Time Series of Option Prices
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the dynamics of crude oil markets proxied by the USO ETF. Based on a preliminary analysis of the time series of implied volatility surfaces, we propose a model accounting for multiple stochastic volatilities, co-jumps, and self-exciting jump intensity. We estimate the model on a time series of option prices using a quasi-Bayesian methodology that exploits sequential Monte Carlo methods. We compare the performances of the proposed model with several nested and nonnested specifications. Our results show that both multiple variance factors and self-excitation in the jumps process are needed for accurate model fitting and to improve out-of-sample forecasting.

title: Desiccation of the Caspian Sea

detail.title: Desiccation of the Caspian Sea
detail.abstract: This essay examines the accelerating desiccation of the Caspian Sea and its multi-dimensional impacts on the surrounding region. Historically characterized by cyclical water level fluctuations, the Caspian is currently facing a critical decline driven by climate change, increased evaporation, and the damming of major inflowing rivers like the Volga. The study explores the concept of "ambulatory coastlines" and the resulting challenges for jurisdictional claims and maritime boundaries among the littoral states. Beyond the environmental catastrophe, the paper analyzes the socioeconomic consequences for local communities, including the decline of the fishing industry and threats to biodiversity. It concludes by emphasizing the urgent need for a coordinated regional response, integrated water management strategies, and international cooperation to mitigate the looming ecological and economic crisis in the Caspian basin.

title: Discrete Taylor Rules

detail.title: Discrete Taylor Rules
detail.abstract: I introduce a discrete Taylor rule that mirrors the institutional practice of adjusting policy rates in 25-basis-point steps. Re-estimating several examples from the literature shows that this rule reduces residuals by up to one-third, suggesting smaller monetary policy shocks than previously estimated. Embedding the rule in a New-Keynesian model and additionally restricting interest rate adjustments to two predetermined dates per quarter reveals three insights: First, the model lacks a steady state and exhibits endogenous cycles. Second, impulse responses are significantly affected by discreteness and are inhomogeneous with respect to the shock size. Third, during a business cycle matching moments of the US economy, the interest rate is on average 74 basis points away from the linear-rule case, which explains 2 % of output gap and 4 % of inflation variance.

title: Subcontracting in Federal Spending: Micro and Macro Implications

detail.title: Subcontracting in Federal Spending: Micro and Macro Implications
detail.abstract:
This paper studies the critical but underexplored role of subcontracting in shaping the spatial and firm-level effects of federal government spending. Using newly available data on defense subcontract awards linked to establishment-level data from NETS, we examine prime–subcontractor relationships across regions, industries, and over time. We document three key facts. First, subcontracting reallocates a substantial share of federal dollars across geographic areas, weakening the link between the location of prime contracts and where spending ultimately occurs. Second, subcontracting shifts spending across industries, notably from service-sector primes to manufacturing subcontractors. Third, large firms dominate subcontracting networks, including by receiving subcontracts from smaller primes. Accounting for geographic reallocation implies that conventional estimates understate local fiscal multipliers by about 20%. Furthermore, local multipliers are smaller for subcontracting than for prime contracting, partly because subcontracted spending is concentrated among large manufacturing firms that exhibit more muted employment responses. Establishment-level evidence further shows that subcontracting generates weaker employment effects, even conditional on firm size and industry, reflecting the less stable nature of subcontracting relationships. Overall, our findings show that subcontracting fundamentally reshapes the transmission of procurement spending through the private sector, with important implications for the local and aggregate effects of federal spending.

detail.title: How Restrictive is U.S. Trade Policy?
detail.abstract:
This short note computes Trade Restrictiveness Index measures for current U.S. trade policy. Building on the ideas of Anderson and Neary (1996, 2005), the Trade Restrictiveness Index is the uniform tariff that leaves the U.S. consumer as well off as under actual policy. As of October 2025, U.S. trade policy is twice as restrictive as headline tariff numbers suggest. The Trade Restrictiveness Index is 23 percent, which stands in contrast to the 11 percent average tariff rate. Trade policy towards Canada and Mexico is two to three times more restrictive than average tariff rates suggest. Sectoral analysis shows that the restrictiveness is concentrated in vehicles, machinery, and electrical equipment.

detail.abstract: This paper examines work-centered social systems such as the German Bürgergeld and the planned Grundsicherung as forms of institutionally organized structural violence. At its core is the thesis that these systems are not merely burdensome for neurodivergent people, but structurally hazardous to health and therefore legally unreasonable. Illness thus appears not as individual failure, but as a predictable system effect of a normative architecture of work and performance that systematically fails to accommodate neurodivergent modes of existence. The analysis is based on a longitudinal auto-ethnographic and artistic-research dataset that has developed over more than thirteen years (“Speed’s Work”), encompassing documented interactions with multiple job centers, medical institutions, social courts, and administrative bodies, and covering various reform phases of work-centered social systems (Hartz IV, Bürgergeld, transition to Grundsicherung). The aim is not statistical representativeness, but the reconstruction of structurally invariant mechanisms of effect. The evaluation identifies six central empirical findings: (1) an institutionally invariant escalation structure that is reproduced independently of individual behavior; (2) systematically enforced masking as an existential adaptation performance; (3) pathologization as a secondary system reaction to structural overload; (4) the independence of health-related harm from individual cooperation or refusal; (5) the resulting structural predictability of health damage; and (6) the epistemic added value of an autistic epistemic position for capturing implicit normative mechanisms of violence. On this basis, an expanded concept of violence is developed that integrates structural, administrative, classist, and ontological violence. The findings are contextualized constitutionally (Art. 1 and Art. 2 of the Basic Law), in terms of human rights (UN Convention on 2 the Rights of Persons with Disabilities), and internationally. The paper argues that work-centered social systems which systematically force neurodivergent people into illness-producing adaptation violate state protective obligations. Illness functions here as an indicator of a systemic misdesign that cannot be remedied through individual case corrections, but only through a structural reconfiguration of welfare-state security.

detail.title: Financial Globalization: Risk Sharing or Risk Exposure?
detail.abstract:
We study how the increased cross-country ownership of financial assets between advanced and emerging economies impacted their financial and macroeconomic volatility. While cross-country ownership improved risk-sharing and reduced volatility associated with financial crises, it also increased the exposure of countries to foreign crises, leading to higher international co-movement. Through quantitative applications of a two-region model representative of advanced and emerging economies, we find that financial globalization reduced volatility worldwide, but significantly more in emerging economies.

detail.abstract: Sparse portfolios are commonly justified by trading frictions or managerial constraints. We show that, even in frictionless markets, sparsity is an economically principled form of complexity control in high-dimensional portfolio choice. Increasing the number of active holdings improves diversification but amplifies finite-sample estimation error. We formalize this tradeoff through an estimation-efficiency frontier that decomposes Sharpe-ratio losses into efficiency losses from restricting the asset set and estimation losses from learning portfolio weights. Under an approximate factor structure, these forces generate a sharp interior optimum for portfolio sparsity, yielding testable predictions for optimal portfolio complexity.

detail.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) and robotics increasingly perform tasks traditionally held by human workers, the debate over "robot taxation" has moved from theoretical speculation to a central pillar of fiscal policy discussion. Proponents argue that taxing robots can mitigate rising wealth inequality and fund the transition for displaced workers, while critics contend such levies stifle innovation and reduce national competitiveness. This paper analyzes the trade-offs between fiscal stability and technological progress, proposing a framework for an "automation-neutral" tax system that shifts the burden from labor to capital without halting the march of productivity.

detail.title: Financial Literacy and Saving Behavior: Global Cross-Sectional Evidence
detail.abstract: Savings play a critical role in both individual financial well-being and economic development. This article examines the impact of financial literacy, income, educational level, and age on saving decisions across 136 countries, using data from the Global Financial Inclusion Database (2021) and employing Generalized Structural Equation Modelling (GSEM). Financial literacy is conceptualized as a latent variable, based on five indicators related to financial knowledge, financial behavior, and financial attitudes, aligned with the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) pillars. The analysis demonstrates that financial literacy is a fundamental driver for saving in the short and long term. Education level and income are consistent predictors of savings, while age exhibits distinct effects depending on the savings objective. Regional differences emerge, with Latin American countries showing the strongest link between financial literacy and savings, whereas in high-income economies, its influence is less pronounced. These findings underscore the multifaceted role of financial literacy in shaping saving decisions and highlight its implications for tailored public policies.

detail.abstract:
We propose a framework for studying financial and macroeconomic dynamics in an environment where liquid assets have a productive use but their supply is limited (i.e., the economy is starved for liquidity). The private demand for financial assets arises from the need to hold them for production. The private supply of financial assets is limited and unstable because of borrowing constraints and default risk. We discuss open-economy applications that analyze the accumulation of foreign reserves by emerging economies, the increase in public debt issued by advanced economies, the rapid growth of emerging economies, structural changes in financial markets, and financial globalization. A key result is that most of these developments led to a decline in interest rates and an increase in global macroeconomic volatility, driven by riskier borrower portfolios.

detail.abstract: The landscape of orthodontic scholarly communication is undergoing a profound and accelerating transformation. This commentary critically examines the convergence of technological, economic, and methodological forces reshaping how orthodontic research is produced, evaluated, and disseminated. Through synthesis of contemporary publishing trends, we identify four interconnected paradigm shifts that form a modern publishing ecosystem: the rapid transition to Open Access models, the emergence of artificial intelligence as both research subject and tool, escalating demands for methodological transparency, and the diversification of knowledge dissemination channels. For the orthodontic community to thrive in this new environment, researchers must evolve beyond traditional scientific roles to become strategic communicators within this interconnected ecosystem.

detail.abstract: In this document we describe a project to link records from the 1940 U.S. Census to records for individuals in the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID). The project is part of a larger effort to conduct parallel linkages to the 1940 Census for respondents to the PSID, the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study (WLS), the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project (NSHAP), and the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS). Each study contains sample members who were alive at the time of the 1940 federal census and were thus enumerated (along with their families and household members). These five ongoing longitudinal studies are central components of America’s data infrastructure for interdisciplinary research on aging and the life course; physical and mental health, disability, and well-being; later-life work, economic well-being, and retirement; end-of-life issues, and many other topics. Adding information about sample members from the 1940 Census expands the utility of all five projects and enables important research on the effects of early life social, economic, environmental, contextual, and other factors on subsequent life outcomes. For a longer discussion of the overall linking project, see Warren, Helgertz, and Xu (2020). Broadly, the project described in this document involved (1) preparing and formatting data files containing cohort members’ identifying information; (2) deploying machine learning algorithms to automatically link survey members to their 1940 U.S. Census record; (3) hand linking records that could not be machine linked and hand-verifying a portion of those that could; and (4) documenting the new measures and making them available as part of the PSID’s restricted access dissemination systems in a manner consistent with the confidentiality protection of PSID sample members. In this document we describe the linking procedures, explain the structure of the resulting linked files and how they can be accessed, and provide information about linkage rates and the reliability and validity of the links.

detail.title: Episodic Factor Pricing
detail.abstract: Conventional factor models assume that factors are stable over time. We challenge this view by showing that factors switch between active and inactive regimes. We propose a real-time method to identify factor active states without look-ahead bias. Factor premia are concentrated primarily in active states and are largely absent otherwise. Conditioning on these states delivers economically and statistically significant out-of-sample performance gains. A stochastic discount factor with state-dependent price of risk provides a superior description of the investment opportunity set, establishing factor pricing as episodic rather than persistent.

detail.abstract: Fluctuation in families’ economic conditions over time are an empirically interesting phenomenon; in fact, they are the raison d'être of household panel studies like the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID). The dynamics of wealth are of particular interest, for instance, to understand families’ ability to smooth consumption during times of economic distress (Deaton 1991). In addition, spend-down of wealth in response to long-term care needs of the elderly or human capital investment needs of the young has been a policy- relevant topic (Scholz and Seshadri 2009). Finally, measures of wealth fluctuation can serve as indicators of macro-economic turbulence, such as in the form of widespread and large wealth losses that occurred during the most recent economic recession (Pfeffer et al. 2013)

detail.title: Scaling Sustainable Investing in Emerging and Developing Economies: Frictions and Opportunities
detail.abstract: Mobilizing private capital at scale is critical for financing sustainable development, particularly in emerging and developing economies (EMDEs), where capital is most needed. We conduct a global survey of senior investment decision-makers across a broad spectrum of capital providers, including asset managers, pension and sovereign wealth funds, development finance institutions, philanthropic investors, and others. The survey provides novel evidence on investors’ risk-return expectations, risk perceptions, and investment practices in EMDEs and in blended finance structures. We document four main findings. First, conditional on investor type, return expectations in EMDEs are comparable to those in developed markets, suggesting that categorical exclusions of EMDE assets might be inefficient. Second, investors’ dominant risk perceptions—particularly currency and political risks—are poorly aligned with the de-risking tools commonly employed in blended finance. Third, prevailing approaches to evaluating blended finance rely on both input- and outcome-based metrics, yet with limited measurement of financial and impact additionality. Fourth, our results highlight organizational and informational frictions, rather than unattractive financial fundamentals, as key barriers to scaling sustainable investing in EMDEs.

detail.abstract: This survey article discusses cases during the prior year, which are decided based on one or more provisions of the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (CISG). The CISG is a United Nations treaty that provides a uniform international sales law. It was adopted in Vienna in 1980 and went into effect in 1988. The CISG governs contracts for the international sale of goods between businesses located in different countries that have ratified the treaty. It has been adopted by 95+ countries, including major trading nations like the United States, China, and most European countries. The CISG governs unless the parties expressly contract otherwise. It governs contract formation, obligations of buyers and sellers, remedies for breach, and passing of risk. It doesn't apply to consumer sales, services contracts, or certain excluded goods like ships or aircraft. This year’s survey includes cases discussing: (1) the applicability of the CISG, (2) the CISG’s preemption of certain tort claims, (3) contract formation, (4) the lack of a formal statute of frauds writing requirement, (5) contract interpretation, (6) conformity of goods, (7) breach of contract, (8) recovery of attorney’s fees, and (9) recovery of prejudgment interest.

detail.abstract: In 2017, the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) added a brief measure to identify older individuals at risk for developing Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias. Because of its brevity and strong predictive power in clinical samples, the AD8 Dementia Screen was selected for inclusion. To our knowledge this is the first time the AD8 has been implemented in a national household study. This technical paper provides background on the AD8 Dementia Screen and assesses its implementation in the PSID. We found that the AD8 Dementia Screen items are highly correlated and scale into a single factor. Item response theory analysis suggests the items discriminate well and misclassification on a latent trait representing cognitive impairment is low based on the standard cutoff of 2 or more. Prevalence estimates are in range with other national surveys that offer more detailed measures (e.g., probable and possible dementia; dementia and cognitive impairment-no dementia). Although concordance with clinical measures could not be explored, the AD8 Dementia Screen has good sensitivity and specificity relative to reports of having a prior diagnosis of a memory-related condition. We also established that the measure has good construct validity; that is, measures of age, activity limitations, and a reported prior diagnosis of a memory-related condition all predict having a score of 2 or more on the AD8. Taken together, these analyses suggest that the AD8 Dementia Screen may be used to distinguish individuals with possible dementia from those with normal cognitive functioning in this long-running national household panel study.

publicationDetails.detailsText: George Mason Law & Economics Research Paper No. 26-01

detail.abstract:
Technological innovation has long been a central driver of competition, consumer choice, and financial inclusion in U.S. consumer financial services. From the advent of standardized credit reporting and automated underwriting to online banking and digital payments, innovation has repeatedly expanded access while reducing costs and discriminatory practices. Today, fintech represents the latest and most consequential wave of this evolution. While some innovations, such as artificial intelligence and alternative data underwriting, are genuinely novel, others, including Earned Wage Access (EWA) and Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL), are modernized versions of well-established financial practices delivered more efficiently through technology.

This article argues that fintech’s benefits accrue most strongly to consumers historically underserved by the traditional financial system, including younger, lower-income, rural, and minority households. Drawing on a broad range of empirical research, it shows that fintech products increase access to credit, reduce reliance on high-cost alternatives, lower transaction costs, and mitigate demographic disparities in pricing and approval rates. Evidence indicates that EWA helps workers smooth income volatility, avoid overdraft fees and payday loans, and improve job retention. BNPL enables consumers to manage liquidity and spread the cost of purchases, usually with no interest, without increasing overall financial distress. Moreover, while critics have expressed concern that both EWA and BNPL could lead to increased financial distress, empirical evidence to date indicates that these speculative concerns are unfounded.

Despite these benefits, fintech innovation faces growing regulatory risks. The article contends that inconsistent and overly burdensome state regulation, arbitrary asset thresholds, and misguided restrictions threaten competition and consumer welfare by raising costs and limiting choice. It concludes that a coherent national regulatory framework—emphasizing competition, proportional oversight, and evidence-based intervention—is essential to preserve fintech’s promise. Properly designed regulation can protect consumers while allowing innovation to flourish, particularly for those with the fewest existing financial options.

detail.title: Understanding The Inflation–Output Relationship Across Business Cycle Phases
detail.abstract: We examine the state dependence of monetary policy transmission and the parameters of the Phillips curve, dynamic IS equation, and Taylor rule across four regimes defined by joint deviations of inflation from the Federal Reserve’s target and output from potential. The analysis uncovers important regime-specific asymmetries. The Taylor principle holds across all four regimes. The systematic policy response to the output gap weakens when inflation is below target but output remains above potential, whereas the response to inflation is broadly similar across regimes. The size of monetary policy shocks is significantly larger when inflation exceeds its target. The Phillips curve steepens when inflation exceeds target and output is above potential, while output sensitivity to interest rate changes declines under high inflation and economic slack. This explains why monetary policy shocks are significantly larger in inflationary booms, but transmission becomes less effective when elevated inflation coincides with economic slack.

detail.abstract: We present novel evidence on the global transmission of monetary policy (MP) surprises via bond funds. Using daily MP surprise measures and a multi-country panel of weekly fund flows, we document that bond fund flows respond systematically to MP surprises. The direction, intensity, and persistence of these responses, however, vary across destination countries, fund investment strategies, and fund domiciles. Furthermore, bond fund flows react not only to domestic MP surprises, but also to foreign MP surprises, indicating cross-border spillovers. We explore two mechanisms driving these responses: the relative importance of MP shocks versus information shocks, and the impact of exchange rate movements on portfolio rebalancing. Our findings highlight the role of nonbank financial intermediaries in global MP transmission.

detail.abstract: This article examines the manufactured cognitive dissonance in how major carbon emitters like RWE simultaneously reject and embrace climate attribution science based on their economic interests. By analysing the Lliuya v. RWE case-where a Peruvian farmer sought compensation as well as declaratory and injunctive relief for climate-related glacier melt threatening his community-the article reveals how RWE contested the 'planetary' logic of attribution science when facing liability for historical emissions, arguing that CO2 molecules cannot be traced through complex atmospheric systems. Yet, RWE relies on this same logic to legitimise its carbon offsetting schemes and claim climate neutrality by 2040. This contradiction exposes how carbon majors exploit planetary biogeochemical connections to expand authority over lands in the Global South as carbon sinks for decarbonising purposes, while evading responsibility for the carbonisation of the atmosphere in the first place. This reveals how 'green' carbon markets embed a 'circular carbon economy' at the expense of a decarbonised one, perpetuating the unequal appropriation of the global carbon budget. By framing the Peruvian Amazon as a carbon 'sink' for offsetting while the Peruvian Andes become a carbon 'sinking' place absorbing climate impacts, the analysis highlights the spatial and temporal displacement of carbon harm inherent in contemporary climate mitigation strategies and calls for a reparative approach to planetary climate justice.

detail.abstract: In the first ten months of 2025, Russian exports fell to $339.8 bn (down 4.3% on 2024) amid a decline in global fuel prices. The share of fuel and energy products in Russian exports fell to 54.9%. Other export groups showed significant recovery growth, most notably in the export of machinery and equipment. Imports remained close to last year's level at $224.4 b (-2.4%), with a decrease in imports of investment goods and an increase in the share of consumer goods. In trade with China, supplies of oil, coal, and heavy distillates declined, but exports of pipeline gas and non-ferrous metals increased. The discount to the price of Russian oil increased to 5.8% in October-November. Supplies of Chinese goods to Russia declined mainly due to a twofold decrease in car imports, while other product categories remained more stable.

detail.title: AI Patents
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) innovation on firm outcomes, industry concentration, and social returns. Using a comprehensive dataset of AI patents from the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, we find that, compared to non-AI innovations, AI patents are primarily used to enhance firms' existing capabilities rather than to explore new technologies. Specifically, they are characteristically exploitative, focusing on process improvements rather than the creation of new products. AI patents are associated with lower marginal firm growth and profitability than non-AI patents. However, despite these lower private returns per patent, AI functions as a General Purpose Technology (GPT) deeply rooted in basic science. It generates significant knowledge spillovers across diverse technological fields. Furthermore, we find that these spillover effects contribute to lower industry concentration in the long run. AI exhibits distinct characteristics that differentiate it from previous GPT wave, such as the Information and Communication Technology (ICT).

detail.title: Supply Shocks and Heterogeneous Macroeconomic Effects: Evidence from Copper
detail.abstract: This paper studies the macroeconomic effects of global copper supply shocks. We identify exogenous disruptions to copper supply using a Bayesian structural VAR of the world copper market that combines sign and narrative restrictions. We then trace the international transmission of the identified shock using a two-step approach based on country-level models for major copper-importing and exporting economies. We find that copper supply shocks raise producer prices and depress industrial activity in importing economies, while exporters benefit from higher world prices through improved terms of trade. Importerexporter status alone is insufficient to characterize exposure: heterogeneity in responses reflects differences in manufacturing copper intensity and buffering capacity through secondary copper production.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we examine directional spillovers of idiosyncratic business cycles between European Union countries using the Diebold and Yilmaz (2012, 2014) methodology, making special emphasis on two complementary classifications: CorePeriphery and Old-New Members. Using forecast error variance decomposition (FEVD) matrices derived from a Time Varying Parameter VAR (TVP-VAR) model on cyclical deviations from zonal aggregates, we document significant asymmetries in the transmission of domestic shocks. The results reveal that (i) Core countries exert dominant influence over the periphery, reflecting aggregate demand effects and position in production chains, (ii) the Old-New asymmetry is substantially larger, suggesting that vertical integration in value chains and differences in productive structure generate greater dependence than geographic factors, (iii) France consistently emerges as the main transmitter of domestic demand shocks, while Denmark emerges as the second main transmitter mainly to Bulgaria and Croatia, and (iv) bidirectionality is greater in Euro Area 12 countries (EA12), reflecting real convergence among founding members. We also analyze these asymmetries under a temporal perspective. We find that asymmetries amplify significantly during crisis periods, with France increasing its spillovers from Pre-Crisis period to COVID+Ukraine period in Euro Area 19 countries (EA19). These findings emphasize the importance of coordinating aggregate demand policies and convergence in productive structures to reduce asymmetric vulnerabilities in the monetary union.

title: Shared Data Redundancies and Cyber Attacks
affiliations: Washington University in Saint Louis, John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: Shared Data Redundancies and Cyber Attacks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This project was initiated jointly with Rodney Garratt. I am grateful for his early input and discussions.

detail.abstract: Redundant data storage safeguards records from cyberattacks, disasters, or negligence. When senders and receivers jointly observe transaction data, redundancy is pairwise: each record is held by exactly two parties. We model data sharing agreements that commit counterparties to restore records after disruptions. Such agreements dominate data autarky but induce free riding and underinvestment in security. We characterize budgetbalanced, state-contingent prices, paid upon recovery, that implement efficient protection and depend on others' investments rather than one's own. We also study a regulated financial infrastructure that can supply an additional security cover but may optimally abstain when it crowds out private protection.

title: Innovation, Technology Standardization and the Value of the Firm
affiliations: HEC Paris - Economics & Decision Sciences, HEC Paris - Economics & Decision Sciences and Banque de France

detail.title: Innovation, Technology Standardization and the Value of the Firm

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banque de France Working Paper No. No. 1031
publicationDetails.journalName: Banque de France Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Technology standards are defined by national and international organizations to select and disseminate the best technologies and practices. Using a measure of patent quality and a novel measure of the semantic proximity between patents and standards documents, this paper exploits the standardization process to disentangle the respective contributions of innovation and diffusion to firm value. Producing a patent increases a firm's book value by 0.8% over the first eight years following the patent grant. However, this value deteriorates when the patent is not incorporated into a standard and diffused. In contrast, only firms whose patent specifications are included in a standard experience an additional increase in firm value of about 0.4% thereafter. Similar results are obtained when examining firms' market-value and net worth. Finally, by studying firm-level productivity and markups, we show that the value gains associated with innovation stem from productivity improvements, whereas those associated with diffusion arise from rent extraction.

title: EST-TabPFN: Enhanced Scalability and Throughput for TabPFN Using Batched Inference and CPU-Optimized Prediction
affiliations: National University of Sciences and Technology, National University of Sciences and Technology, Pakistan and National University of Sciences and Technology, Pakistan - NUST Business School

detail.title: EST-TabPFN: Enhanced Scalability and Throughput for TabPFN Using Batched Inference and CPU-Optimized Prediction
detail.abstract: TabPFN is a transformer-based prediction model that makes quick predictions on small datasets. According to recent studies, applying TabPFN to real-world imbalanced datasets often led to high resource usage and unstable inference. In response, our paper introduces an improved workflow called EST-TabPFN. This proposed workflow adds a more efficient prediction method, continuous CPU monitoring, and a stable batched inference process. We tested this approach with the Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset [1](Dal Pozzolo et al., 2015). We have tested EST-TabPFN using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and prediction time on test sets ranging from 5,000 to 100,000 samples. The results show that EST-TabPFN provides steady accuracy, faster processing, and noticeably smoother CPU performance compared to the limitations reported by [2](Hollmann et al. 2023). This resulted in an expansion of the original TabPFN's adaptability in CPU-friendly environments. Our suggested workflow EST-TabPFN is uploaded on an open-source GITHUB repository [3](EST-TabPFN, 2025). This proposed workflow is an application of preprocessing and batching on TabPFN workflow to enhance its performance in resource-constrained environments and gauge its performance on real-world imbalanced datasets.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how dispersion in banks' subjective inflation forecasts is a channel of the transmission of monetary policy to credit supply. We extend the Monti-Klein model of monopolistic banking by incorporating risk aversion, subjective beliefs, and ambiguity aversion. The model predicts that greater inflation uncertainty or asymmetry in beliefs raises equilibrium loan rates and amplifies credit rationing. Using AnaCredit loan-level data for France, we estimate finite-mixture density regressions that allow for latent heterogeneity in loan pricing. Empirically, we find that higher subjective uncertainty and asymmetry both increase average lending rates and skew their distribution, disproportionately affecting financially constrained firms in the right tail. Quantitatively, moving from the 25th to the 75th percentile of our indicators raises average borrowing costs by more than 10 basis points, which translates into roughly 0.5 billion euros of additional annual interest expenses for nonfinancial corporations. By contrast, forecast disagreement has a weaker and less systematic effect. Taken together, these results show that uncertainty and asymmetry in inflation expectations are independent and powerful drivers of credit conditions, underscoring their importance for understanding monetary policy transmission through the banking sector.

title: Conceptual Thinking and Machine Learning

detail.title: Conceptual Thinking and Machine Learning
detail.abstract: The paper combines methods from conceptual thinking and machine learning in order to enhance the analytic performance of machine learning. The approach is applied to the ubiquitous challenge of defining faults in operating systems which essential in diagnostics and prognostics embedded in digital twins. Conceptual thinking consists of methods for learning and explaining used in education. These have been developing over two decades, with applications in a dozen countries educational systems. Machine learning, and in particular deep learning, was developed in the past decade with significant results in predictive analytics, in many disciplines. Up front, the ideas underlying machine-learning methods bare similarities to methods for learning and explaining concepts. Here, the relationship between machine learning and conceptual thinking methods is studied and discussed with an engineering perspective. Three new methods based on conceptual thinking are presented and implemented in machine learning. These methods enable complex insights to be presented by content experts using graphs and text, even when mathematical models are sometimes limited. It enhances the capabilities of data centric engineering.

detail.title: Subordination: A Functional and Theoretical Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: Duke Law School Public Law & Legal Theory Series Forthcoming

detail.abstract: There has been no serious scholarship on subordination since a 1961 Yale Law Journal article which described subordination as then utilized and discussed how it applied in practice. This Article updates and, in scope, goes beyond that earlier article, analyzing subordination not only from a functional but also from a theoretical perspective. The Article classifies and compares the various types of subordination--contractual, structural, equitable, and statutory--and examines their rationales and uses. It then analyzes and critiques the legal frameworks for subordination, showing that courts remain profoundly confused about some of subordination's basics, let alone its sometimes arcane and inconsistent terminology. Finally, the Article analyzes how subordination law should be improved, including by systematizing its terminology, settling its judicial splits, and, more generally, resolving doctrinal confusion.

title: Patriarchy And Gender Inequality In Late Ottoman Palestine (1880s-1910s): Spousal Age Gaps In A Multi-Layered Society
affiliations: Ruhr-University Bochum, University of Tübingen - Department of Economics, Ruhr-University Bochum, Ruhr-University Bochum and Cardinal Stefan Wyszynski University

detail.title: Patriarchy And Gender Inequality In Late Ottoman Palestine (1880s-1910s): Spousal Age Gaps In A Multi-Layered Society
detail.abstract: For this study, we created the first large-scale dataset for Palestine ca. 1880-1910 that informs about the gender age gap at marriage, where the man is typically older, a widely used indicator of gender inequality. The average age gap in Palestine was relatively high (6.6 years), in most places in Europe age gaps were lower, whereas it was higher in other parts of the Eastern Mediterranean. Among potential correlates, couples with a herding background had lower age gaps. Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe also had lower gender gaps, i.e. lower gender inequality. Muslim and Orthodox couples exhibited the highest age gaps (6.7 years), while other Christian and Jewish communities had lower marriage age gaps, and hence probably lower gender inequality.

title: How Multidimensional Distances Affects the Global Trading Patterns Of Cobalt Products
affiliations: , , , ,  and

detail.title: How Multidimensional Distances Affects the Global Trading Patterns Of Cobalt Products
detail.abstract: Cobalt mineral resource is highly concentrated in a few countries while it’s widely applied in multiple key fields and plays a significant role in the high-end manufacturing industries. In order to explore the global supply pattern of cobalt mineral products, this paper selects 3 products from the upstream and midstream segments of the cobalt industry and constructs the global trade network using the global trade data in 2015-2024. Based on the complex network theory, the global trade structure of cobalt products in the last decade is explored both from the perspective of the entire network and the perspective of the individual nodes. Furthermore, to further explore the influencing factors of global cobalt products trade, 4 dimensional distance matrixes are constructed respectively to perform correlation and linear regression analysis by QAP(Quadratic Assignment Procedure) method. The results show that: the structure of world’s cobalt products trade is extremely unbalanced especially for the up-stream product. The COVID-19 pandemic has severely affected the trade structure of cobalt products. Major countries like the USA, China Germany and the UK tend to enhance its importance within the network by simultaneously acting as both a major importer and a major exporter. The QAP correlation and regression analysis results show that geographical distance and economic transaction distance normally wouldn’t affect the trade of cobalt mid-stream products while the economic distance and the distance of the transaction price show significant impact to the trade of cobalt products.

title: Endogenous Criticality and the 2^N Lattice: A Deterministic Metric for Finite-Time Singularities in Financial Markets

detail.title: Endogenous Criticality and the 2^N Lattice: A Deterministic Metric for Finite-Time Singularities in Financial Markets
detail.abstract: Didier Sornette’s Log-Periodic Power Law (LPPL) identifies financial bubbles as "Finite- Time Singularities" driven by positive feedback loops. This paper proposes a geometricfoundation for these critical phenomena: the 2^N Lattice Theory. We argue that the super-exponential growth of a bubble is constrained by a pre-existing binary grid (2^N). The "Dragon King" (extreme crash) is not an outlier, but a deterministic event triggeredwhen price momentum collides with the rigorous boundaries of the hidden lattice. Weintroduce the "Spike Bar" as the observable signal of this collision, offering a simplified, non-stochastic method for predicting critical turning points.

detail.title: The Impact of "Green Regulation" on Firms' Innovation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banque de France Working Paper No. 1016
publicationDetails.journalName: Banque de France Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper analyses the effect of "green regulations" i.e. those aimed at mitigating the effects of climate change and environmental externalities, on innovation, using a novel regulatory database covering the period 2008-2022 for Spain. The database identifies regulations at both the national and regional levels through textual analysis. Employing a panel data approach, we assess how different types of environmental regulations-particularly those related to renewable energy-affect firm-level innovation activities. Our findings indicate that national level green regulations have a positive effect on innovation, whereas regional level regulations show mixed or negligible impacts. Importantly, the interaction between national and regional regulations, measuring the simultaneous production of legal texts at both levels can foster innovation but at a reduced pace with respect to the sole production of regulation at the national level. Given the results for regional-level regulation, our results provide evidence in favour of the hypothesis that regulatory fragmentation due to unequal, overlapping, inconsistent or conflicting procedure across jurisdictions may diminish these benefits.

title: Skipping the Factory: Service-Led Growth and Structural Transformation in the Developing World
affiliations: Yale University - Department of Economics, Yale University and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), Yale University

detail.title: Skipping the Factory: Service-Led Growth and Structural Transformation in the Developing World
detail.abstract:
In today’s developing world, many economies appear to bypass industrialization and transition directly from agriculture to services. The largest rise in service employment has occurred in non-tradable consumer services, such as retail and hospitality, especially in urban areas, where many cities resemble consumer hubs built around local demand. These patterns of growth raise fundamental questions: Can service-led growth sustain a growth of living standards over time? Is service-led growth inherently biased toward affluent urban consumers? What role should policy play? We propose a parsimonious general equilibrium framework that incorporates non-homothetic preferences and locally non-tradable consumer services. Our framework bridges macro and micro perspectives, and enables counterfactual and welfare analysis that accounts for both individual and spatial heterogeneity. We relate our framework to the recent literature and suggest several extensions and directions of future research.

detail.title: Global Sectoral Supply Shocks, Inflation, and Monetary Policy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banque de France Working Paper No. 1026

detail.abstract: We identify two global supply shocks that generate tensions in supply chains: shocks to transportation services and shocks to the production of highly specific intermediate inputs. Using a structural vector autoregression identified with sign, narrative, and boundary restrictions, we exploit their distinct implications for transportation costs. Transportation shocks raise shipping costs, while input production shocks lower equilibrium transportation prices by reducing output and demand for complementary services. Complementing the analysis with a global demand shock, we construct structurally interpretable, monthly indices for supply-side tensions and demand-induced congestion along global supply chains from 1969 to 2024. Both global supply shocks generate recessionary and inflationary effects in U.S. data but differ markedly in persistence and magnitude. Input production shocks produce large and persistent effects and elicit partial monetary policy accommodation, whereas transportation shocks are transitory and largely looked through.

title: Customer Overlap and Diversion Ratios
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Economics, Stanford University and Stanford University

detail.title: Customer Overlap and Diversion Ratios
detail.abstract:
We define the concept of customer overlap of product j with product k as the share of j's customers who buy k. We then argue that, in appropriate contexts, customer overlaps are an excellent proxy for diversion ratios, a useful and popular way to summarize competition between sellers of substitute products. Unlike diversion ratios, which are often challenging to estimate, customer overlaps are straightforwardly observed in many data sets. We show theoretically, and then validate empirically, the close connection between customer overlaps and diversion ratios. We then illustrate the potential use of customer overlap in contexts where estimation of diversion ratios could be prohibitive.

title: The Erckenbrack Model of Adoption A Scale-and Timing-Sensitive Theory of Technology Adoption and Authority Loss

detail.title: The Erckenbrack Model of Adoption A Scale-and Timing-Sensitive Theory of Technology Adoption and Authority Loss

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This document introduces the Erckenbrack Model of Adoption, a novel, general theory of technology adoption that departs fundamentally from classical diffusion, acceptance, and cost-benefit models. The model demonstrates that beyond critical thresholds of scale, timing, and coordination, technology adoption ceases to be a voluntary efficiency choice and becomes a structural constraint. Crucially, the model shows that failure to adopt does not preserve autonomy or authority, but instead accelerates relative authority loss through endogenous penalties. These penalties-decision latency, competitive exclusion, and strategic irrelevance-are scale-sensitive, activate sequentially, and culminate in irreversible authority transfer. A formal mathematical representation is provided to show how adoption asymmetry emerges once these thresholds are crossed.

title: The Geography of Science
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley and

detail.title: The Geography of Science
detail.abstract:
Science has long been concentrated in the Western world, but the global research landscape is undergoing a profound reorganization. Using data on 44 million publications from 1980 to 2022, we document the geography of science in terms of who produces it, what it studies, and where it diffuses. The share of publications produced in the United States has fallen from 40% in 1980 to 15% in 2022, while China’s share has risen from near-zero to 32%. This pattern extends even to elite outlets, with China now producing over 35% of top-journal publications. Notably, this is driven not only by an expanding researcher base but also—to a large extent—by increases in individual productivity. This growth varies by fields: China leads in the Engineering and Physical Sciences (such as Chemistry), while the US retains its lead in Biomedical and Health Sciences. Moreover, China’s expanding leadership in scientific production has not translated into a commensurate shift in global diffusion and integration. Elite research remains disproportionately focused on US topics (40% of breakthrough publications), and citations to Chinese research disproportionately come from within China rather than from other regions, even for top-tier science. Similar to China, other middle- and low-income countries (including India, Russia, and Brazil) have also expanded output producing as much research as high-income European Union countries combined (about 21% overall) but they remain underrepresented in top-tier journals. Overall, our findings highlight both the democratization and fragmentation of global science, raising important questions about the future of the global scientific enterprise.

title: Capital Misallocation and Risk Sharing
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison, University of Minnesota - Minneapolis - Department of Economics, University of Illinois Urbana Champaign and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK)

detail.title: Capital Misallocation and Risk Sharing
detail.abstract: We develop an optimal contracting model in which limited enforcement of financial contracts generates dispersion in marginal products of capital across firms. We show that the optimal contract can be implemented using state-contingent transfers and a simple collateral constraint that limits the capital input of firms by a fraction of the financial wealth of the firm owner. Compared to models with exogenous collateral constraint and incomplete markets (for example Moll (2014)), we find that the degree of measured misallocation is increasing in the persistence of the idiosyncratic productivity shocks. Under the optimal contract, the possibility to transfer wealth from high productivity states to low productivity states allows firm owners to trade off efficient allocation of consumption against the efficient allocation of capital. We show that for reasonable values of risk aversion, insurance needs more than offset production efficiency concerns.

title: Inefficient Market Depth

detail.title: Inefficient Market Depth
detail.abstract: A trader who uses a limit order, instead of a market order, saves the bid-ask spread but incurs an execution delay. Wide-spread limit orders usage increases market depth and apparently enhances market quality. Yet, it also postpones gains from trade realization, eventually impairing welfare. I design a dynamic equilibrium model of limit order market, and I show that market depth and limit order execution delays are related positively, and both negatively with welfare. Indeed, inefficient market depth arising from orders inefficiently queuing in the book, coincides with excessive execution delays. In practice, the limit order execution delays should be taken into consideration for a comprehensive assessment of market quality.

title: Why is the Mental Health of the Youngest American Workers in Decline?
affiliations: Dartmouth College - Department of Economics and University College London

detail.title: Why is the Mental Health of the Youngest American Workers in Decline?
detail.abstract:
The worsening mental health of young workers in the United States drives the disappearance of the U-shape in wellbeing and the hump-shape in illbeing in the last decade. Illbeing declines in age among workers but is hump-shaped among non-workers across all US states. This has been the case for some time and is apparent in our analyses of two large US datasets with long time runs - the Behavioral Risk Survey System 1993-2025 and the National Health Interview Survey of 1997-2024. Although the mental health of workers and non-workers has been declining it has been deteriorating most quickly among young workers, leading to a steepening in the age gradient of mental illbeing for workers. Improvements in worker wellbeing (and declines in worker illbeing) with age are mirrored in age differences in reported working conditions in the American Job Quality Survey of 2025: six measures of job quality rise with age. Declines in mental health are most pronounced among the youngest workers ages 18-22 who are likely drawn from lower socio-economic classes and report the greatest difficulties making ends meet.

title: SNAP Work Requirements, Administrative Burden and Procedural Denials
affiliations: University of Utah,  and

detail.title: SNAP Work Requirements, Administrative Burden and Procedural Denials
detail.abstract:
Work requirements are often criticized for imposing administrative burdens that reduce access to benefits, yet prior research has struggled to isolate this mechanism from other sources of disenrollment. This paper provides direct evidence by examining procedural denials in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). We study work requirements for Able-Bodied Adults Without Dependents (ABAWDs) and exploit age-based exemptions that apply to individuals aged 50 and older. Using administrative data and difference-in-differences models leveraging waiver periods, we find that work requirements significantly increase procedural and overall denials. Our results indicate that these policies deter participation through imposed administrative burdens.

title: What is Forensic Finance?
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin - Department of Finance and University of Texas at Austin - Department of Finance

detail.title: What is Forensic Finance?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Foundations and Trends in Finance, Forthcoming

detail.abstract: We survey a growing field studying aspects of finance that are potentially illegal, illicit, or immoral. Some of the literature is investigative in nature to uncover malfeasance that is recent and possibly ongoing. Other forensic finance research examines past events to generate a fuller understanding of the activities, economic magnitudes, incentives, and players involved. The work spans newer areas such as cryptocurrencies, financial advisor and broker misconduct, and greenwashing; and newer research in established fields that are still developing, such as insider trading, structured finance, market manipulation, political connections, public finance, and corporate fraud. We highlight investigative forensic finance, common economic questions, common empirical methods, industry and political opposition, censoring, and the importance of avoiding publication biases. Compared to other finance papers, forensic work has similar citations and SSRN downloads, and more media and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) citations. Along with prominent examples of industry reform and awareness, this highlights the potential for real-world impact. By laying out commonalities in research themes, questions, methods, and approaches across fields that may at first seem disparate, we hope to encourage more investigation of incentives and mechanisms in darker corners of finance.

title: The Distributional Effects of Cost-Sharing in a Universal Healthcare System
affiliations: , Statistics Norway and Yale University

detail.title: The Distributional Effects of Cost-Sharing in a Universal Healthcare System
detail.abstract:
Patient cost-sharing is used as a tool to limit over-utilization of insured healthcare services in almost all high-income countries. We study its distributional consequences in the context of a publicly-funded universal health insurance system, where consumers (as tax-payers) are residual claimants on insurer spending. We highlight the distinction between consumers' elasticity of demand for healthcare services—which moderates how cost-sharing rules affect healthcare utilization—and their baseline level of demand—which moderates how cost-sharing rules affect out-of-pocket costs. Using detailed administrative data on the Norwegian national health insurance scheme, we study a 2010 policy change that raised the age threshold for cost-sharing exemption, thereby increasing patient cost-sharing substantially for adolescents. We find that females and native-born Norwegians have higher average utilization and thus have more at stake financially from cost-sharing, but are relatively less responsive to cost-sharing. In contrast, lower-income individuals as well as individuals with a chronic health condition have both higher average healthcare utilization as well as higher responsiveness. Cost-sharing therefore places a larger burden on these groups both in terms of the financial cost of out-of-pocket spending and in terms of reduced quantities of healthcare used.

title: Party Pressure and Representation
affiliations: University of Miami

detail.title: Party Pressure and Representation
detail.abstract:
I study how political parties affect representation in the U.S. House. To do so, I account for party pressure on the votes of members in an otherwise standard spatial model that uses roll call voting patterns to identify member ideologies. I simultaneously estimate voter ideologies from survey responses, leveraging their responses on issues before Congress to bridge voters and members into the same ideological space. I find that, relative to a model without party pressure, member ideologies and those of their constituents are much more closely aligned. The results imply that, in terms of actual votes, parties drive a wedge between members and those they represent. I provide evidence that parties do so strategically, balancing the need for legislative wins and the electoral concerns of their members.

title: Monopsony, Markdowns, and Minimum Wages
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt, Institute for Employment Research (IAB) and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Monopsony, Markdowns, and Minimum Wages
detail.abstract:
This paper presents the first direct test of two interlinked predictions at the core of the monopsony theory of the labor market: (i) that firms exploit wage-setting power by marking down wages below the marginal revenue product of labor, and (ii) that exogenous wage constraints, if binding, eliminate markdowns. Our research design revisits the 2015 introduction of a high minimum wage in Germany. Drawing on a monopsony model, we derive an empirically tractable difference-in-differences specification that provides a quantitative benchmark for the firm-level markdown response. Our main result is that empirical markdowns respond only 0–25% as much as the monopsony model would have predicted. Hence, at least for the labor market segment we study, (i) markdowns largely reflect other distortions than monopsony, (ii) markdowns are mismeasured, (iii) minimum wages induce widespread labor shortages, or (iv) the standard monopsony model does not provide a full, realistic account of the labor market.

detail.abstract: This paper studies when issuing a dollar-backed stablecoin is privately viable for a regulated commercial bank. We develop a parsimonious partial-equilibrium model in which stablecoin issuance expands the bank's balance sheet, requires backing with highquality liquid assets, and interacts with liquidity and capital regulation. Profitability depends on whether stablecoins substitute for costly wholesale funding or cannibalize low-cost deposits, on the degree of balance-sheet consolidation, and on the interestrate environment through deposit-rate pass-through. We derive a simple profitability condition showing that issuance is viable only when funding savings exceed the net interest margin drag and regulatory costs of reserve backing. Comparative statics imply that issuance declines with consolidation intensity and deposit cannibalization and is most constrained at low nominal interest rates. A calibration using U.S. banking data illustrates that profitable issuance occurs only over a narrow range of monetary and balance-sheet conditions and is more likely under partial deconsolidation or greater wholesale-funding substitution.

title: DualS-GNN: A Dual-Stream Graph Neural Network Integrating Semantic and Structural Information
affiliations: Army Engineering University, Army Engineering University, Army Engineering University, Army Engineering University, Army Engineering University and Army Engineering University

detail.title: DualS-GNN: A Dual-Stream Graph Neural Network Integrating Semantic and Structural Information
detail.abstract: Knowledge graph reasoning is used to infer missing facts or relations from graph structured data. Graph neural networks have shown significant advantages in handling related tasks of graph-structured data due to their unique message-passing mechanisms.However, existing methods often exhibit certain limitations. Although some GNNs can capture deep topological dependencies through complex mechanisms such as subgraph aggregation, they fail to adequately incorporate textual semantics. Others, while introducing rich textual features via pre-trained language models, typically confine their structural modeling to shallow neighborhood aggregation, lacking the capacity for deep reasoning.To this end, this paper proposes a novel Graph neural network called DualS-GNN, which enhances its reasoning capability by integrating both textual semantic information and structural information from knowledge graphs.Specifically, the model utilizes a pre-trained language model and a directed path subgraph to respectively acquire textual semantic information and structural information of the graph-structured data.Then, an efficient feature processing module and a residual module are adopted to combine these two kinds of information to further enhance the nodes' expressive capability of the nodes. Experiments demonstrate that DualS-GNN has a strong ability to capture and enhance node features, and it demonstrates excellent performance in inference tasks under various types of datasets.The code implementation is available in https://github.com/SanjinCabbage/Duals-GNN.

title: Complementarity between stated and revealed preferences in pedestrian route choice: Evidence from a university campus living lab in Kampala
affiliations: Makerere University, Makerere University, Ndejje University, Makerere University,  and

detail.title: Complementarity between stated and revealed preferences in pedestrian route choice: Evidence from a university campus living lab in Kampala
detail.abstract: Walking is the most pervasive form of urban mobility, yet pedestrian route choice remains insufficiently understood in dense urban environments where efficiency, comfort, and environmental quality interact. This study advances pedestrian route choice modelling by jointly analyzing stated preference (SP) and revealed preference (RP) data, using Makerere University as a living laboratory. As a large academic institution embedded within Kampala’s urban fabric, the campus typifies concentrated activity hubs characterized by heterogeneous infrastructure, varied environmental conditions, and diverse pedestrian behaviour. The study develops separate SP and RP discrete choice models alongside a complementarity between SP and RP behaviour in individual decision-making, by examining how pedestrians trade off travel time, slope, greenery, amenities, and pedestrian infrastructure. Model robustness and predictive performance are evaluated through repeated hold-out validation using a 70/30 estimation–validation split, following Apollo’s out-of-sample assessment procedure. Results reveal systematic divergences between stated and observed behaviour: while SP responses suggest a preference for shorter and more direct routes, RP data show that pedestrians often accept longer paths to access greener, less congested, or higher-quality walking environments. Greenery and amenities consistently enhance route attractiveness, while slope exerts a stronger deterrent effect for female pedestrians. The joint SP+RP model outperforms individual SP and RP models, exhibiting greater parameter stability and the smallest out-of-sample log-likelihood differences, indicating superior generalizability. These findings highlight the value of integrating SP and RP data to capture realistic pedestrian decision-making and reduce hypothetical bias. Future research should extend this integrated framework to larger urban networks and incorporate additional behavioural factors such as perceived safety, crowding, and temporal dynamics to inform pedestrian-oriented planning.

publicationDetails.journalName: New York University Stern School of Business Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies how artificial intelligence influences asset prices by altering the elasticity of institutional demand. We focus on AI as a firm-side production and organizational technology, captured by institutional exposure to AI-intensive firms. Embedding this exposure into a demand-system asset-pricing framework, we show that technological change inside firms is a structural determinant of demand elasticity, price impact, and return dynamics. Rather than increasing demand elasticity, exposure to AI-intensive firms is associated with steeper institutional demand, reflecting increased valuation uncertainty and the importance of long-horizon beliefs that lead institutions to rebalance less aggressively. Using Form 13F holdings merged with CRSP and Compustat data, we find that AI exposure-especially among banks-reduces market elasticity and amplifies equilibrium price impact. Event-based evidence from the public release of ChatGPT further shows that AI-related valuation shocks dissipate more slowly when institutional demand is inelastic.

detail.abstract: Many ideas show remarkable returns in small-scale trials but often disappoint when scaled to broader populations and contexts. Using early childhood investment as a case study, this study develops a dynamic human capital formation model that integrates complementary skill investment with "Option C thinking" on scaling challenges. The model is stylized in the Chicago tradition: micro-founded with optimizing agents, dynamic skill production, and a policymaker evaluating scaling decisions. It formalizes how naive extrapolation from pilot studies systematically overestimates policy efficacy by ignoring "voltage drops," declining treatment effects due to unrepresentativeness at scale. The model demonstrates that optimal scaling policy requires mechanism-based design that anticipates these failures through backward induction from implementation realities. The scientific insights from a set of recent studies provide valuable perspectives on the model.

detail.abstract:
This Article tackles the ubiquitous problem of employer-drafted "disclaimers." Disclaimers are standardized provisions, found in a variety of human resources documents, that confirm employees' at-will status. They typically preserve employers' right to change the terms of employment at any time, sometimes without advance notice. The most careful disclaimers also renounce the legal significance of contrary statements or promises by supervisors and other managerial agents, thus foreclosing contractual obligations that would otherwise arise. Meanwhile employers scrupulously preserve the legal enforceability of terms they desire such as restrictive covenants and arbitration agreements.

Currently there is no defensible legal framework for assessing employment disclaimers, nor has there been any meaningful theoretical engagement with their contractual status. Most courts simply treat these disclaimers as prima facie valid. As a result, employers not only avoid liability for specific commitments, they effectively remove one side of the employment relationship from the realm of contract. Our Article argues that courts defer too readily to disclaimers, and despite purported reliance on contract principles, their deferential approach is not doctrinally compelled.

We propose instead a holistic framework more suitable to the unique characteristics of employment contracts. This approach draws on three aspects of mainstream contract law and theory: (1) a robust literature that questions the validity of assent to consumer contract boilerplate; (2) interpretive canons and contextualist techniques that construe contract language against the drafter and in conformity with the reasonable expectations of the weaker party; and (3) doctrines such as unconscionability and the duty of good faith that impose modest but meaningful substantive limits on drafting. These prescriptions are particularly appropriate in light of employment’s “hyper-relational” character, in which the parties’ obligations are never expressed in a final, formal writing. We propose a holistic treatment of disclaimers that acknowledges them as just one source of governing terms that must ultimately be reconciled with (and potentially subordinated to) conflicting expressions of commitment and nonwaivable common law obligations. In short, we aim to free employment contract law from the tyranny of exculpatory boilerplate.
