detail.abstract: This chapter presents a tractable framework for the study of technology adoption and diffusion in the context of economic development. Firms in countries behind the world technology frontier can rapidly adopt new techniques from the world frontier. Lower absorptive capacity (because of weak education systems, poor management practices, or barriers to technology adoption), institutional distortions, mismatch between frontier technologies and the needs of firms in the country (i.e., "inappropriate technology"), and credit market frictions slow down technology adoption and cause the economy in question to have a greater distance to the frontier and thus lower income per capita-although the long-run growth rate of the country still remains equal to that of the frontier. This framework is extended to study the choice between innovation and imitation, as well as the role of selection for higher-productivity and higher-absorptive capacity firms during the process of economic development. We illustrate the main comparative statics of our framework with a number of correlations based on crosscountry and firm-level data. The tractability of the framework makes it amenable to a range of additional extensions.

title: An Empirical Study of Disaster Related Consumer Behavioral Shifts on Business Marketing Strategies in Sri Lanka

detail.title: An Empirical Study of Disaster Related Consumer Behavioral Shifts on Business Marketing Strategies in Sri Lanka
detail.abstract: Disruptions such as pandemics, economic crises, floods and other major disasters significantly transform consumer purchasing behavior, especially in emerging economies such as Sri Lanka. This research seeks to examine and empirically investigate the impact of disasters and crises on business marketing strategies in the Sri Lankan context. Drawing upon previous research that provides country-level evidence on how economic crises have restructured household food consumption patterns, this research defines major behavioral shift such as panic buying, stockpiling and consumer focus shifting towards basic necessities during times of disaster. Such behavioral shifts generate substantial pressure for companies to revise their pricing, product, and distribution strategies in response to maintain market stability and consumer confidence. By examining the linkage between crisis-induced consumer behavior and strategic marketing responses, this study provides a new contribution to the disaster and marketing literature, and also provides practical implications for businesses operating in disaster-prone and crisis-affected environments such as Sri Lanka.

title: Data-Based Development Theory: Integrating Data Capability into Development Economics

detail.title: Data-Based Development Theory: Integrating Data Capability into Development Economics
detail.abstract: This paper explains why countries with relatively similar levels of capital accumulation, human capital, technological access, and institutional reform nonetheless exhibit pronounced differences in productivity growth and structural transformation. Existing development theories, while clarifying the roles of foundational factors, have not fully explained the mechanisms through which these factors are dynamically coordinated, learned, and adjusted in increasingly complex and information-intensive economies.To address this gap, the paper develops a data-based development theory that conceptualizes data as a system-level cognitive capability. The theory posits that data influences development through three core mechanisms: information-based resource allocation, endogenous learning, and institutional adaptability. In doing so, the study extends development economics by reframing development as a dynamic learning process in the data era. The paper contributes to development economics by offering a conceptual framework that integrates growth, learning, and institutions through the lens of data capacity.

detail.abstract:
The global financial ecosystem is entering an era of unprecedented cryptographic vulnerability, where the mathematical foundations of digital trust are being systematically undermined by the maturation of quantum information science. Decentralized Finance (DeFi), which as of late 2025 manages approximately USD 160 billion in total value locked (TVL) and secures ecosystems like Ethereum with market capitalizations exceeding USD 700 billion, is uniquely exposed to these emerging threats.1 Unlike legacy financial institutions that can rely on legal recourse or central bank intervention to mitigate technological failures, DeFi’s security is entirely derived from its cryptographic primitives. These primitives—primarily the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) and the RSA cryptosystem—are fundamentally susceptible to Shor’s algorithm, which can derive private keys from public keys in polynomial time, rendering the current DeFi architecture obsolete.2
As the industry looks toward the 2050–2060 horizon, the challenge is not merely a technical migration of signature schemes but a fundamental re-architecting of market design and liquidity. This research paper explores the transition to "Lattice-Based Liquidity" (LBL), a paradigm where financial depth and capital formation are intrinsically tied to the performance and security of lattice-based cryptography. This paradigm shifts the view of cryptography from a passive security layer to an active economic primitive that dictates the costs.

title: The Death of Insider Trading Alpha: Most Returns Occur Before Public Disclosure

detail.title: The Death of Insider Trading Alpha: Most Returns Occur Before Public Disclosure

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Insider trading strategies are widely believed to generate abnormal returns, yet practitioner backtests often report performance far exceeding what is documented in the academic literature. Using insider transaction data from U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Form 4 filings for Russell 2000 constituents, we show that this discrepancy is driven by the timing of trade entry. We distinguish between the insider's transaction date, when information remains private, and the filing date, when it becomes publicly available. Strategies that enter on the transaction date generate extremely high Sharpe ratios, but these returns are not economically meaningful. Once entry is delayed until the filing date-the earliest point at which a public investor can legally trade-measured performance collapses, with 70-80 percent of total alpha dissipating between the transaction date and the following trading day, well before any public disclosure. By the time a Form 4 filing is released, the remaining signal is largely confirmatory rather than informative, indicating that backtests relying on transaction dates measure the value of private information rather than a tradable investment strategy.

detail.abstract: Effective appraisal of public investment projects hinges on rigorous preparation, inter-agency coordination, and realistic costing. This case study examines Bangladesh's institutional appraisal process through the Development Project Proposal (DPP) lifecycle and the Project Evaluation Committee (PEC), drawing on official guidelines and practitioner experience. It documents how DPPs are prepared, screened by Project Scrutiny Committees, and refined through PEC deliberations that function as a problem-solving forum rather than a mere gatekeeping step. The analysis highlights recurring appraisal challenges including cost optimism, uneven feasibility studies, project overlap, and capacity constraints exacerbated by ADP/RADP time pressures. It distills actionable lessons: strengthen upstream feasibility and logical frameworks, standardize and enforce appraisal formats (Working Paper, MAF, SAF), introduce independent reviews for large projects, and invest in institutional capacity for design, procurement, and implementation management. Beyond Bangladesh, the study offers comparative insights for developing countries seeking to improve public investment management under institutional and fiscal constraints. By foregrounding process over project-level outcomes, the paper contributes a practitioner-oriented perspective on how appraisal mechanisms can raise project quality and safeguard value for money.

title: Why AI Implementation Fails at Scale: A Comparative, Boundary-Spanning Synthesis

detail.title: Why AI Implementation Fails at Scale: A Comparative, Boundary-Spanning Synthesis
detail.abstract:
Despite unprecedented investment, organisational adoption of artificial intelligence has not translated into proportional, sustained impact. Across independent research, analyst studies, consulting surveys, and regulatory frameworks, a consistent pattern emerges: AI initiatives proliferate, pilots succeed locally, yet enterprise-level value remains elusive. This paper synthesises evidence from these distinct literatures to argue that prevailing explanations—centred on leadership, culture, skills, or ethical readiness—are secondary to a set of recurring structural misalignments in how authority, learning, legitimacy, governance cadence, and ownership are designed and sequenced. The contribution reframes AI implementation as an organisation design problem, clarifying why familiar remedies from prior digital and innovation waves often misfire and identifying the architectural conditions under which AI can become governable at scale.

Supplementary appendices provide a structured comparative matrix and study summaries to support transparency, replication, and reuse of the evidence base underlying the synthesis.

detail.abstract: The stability of the international monetary system is increasingly challenged by the structural limits inherent in the dollar's global dominance. Drawing on the theory in Chapter 2, this paper first examines the limits surrounding monetary hegemony. Chapter 3 features a political economy debate and analysis of the dollar's structural instability from center-left Keynesian and Marxist positions including discussion on the contested dollar dominance in international trade reserves. The paper contends that while the rise of BRICS is a positive indicator of a meaningful step towards monetary multipolarity, the systemic financial structures still tie major currencies to U.S. financial state of affairs, especially the RMB. Integrating theoretical discussions and empirical research of RMB-USD dynamics in Chapter 4, the paper delivers an understanding of the presence of hegemonic influence in international finance.

title: Structural Hysteresis in Directive-Gradient Systems: Thousand-Fold Amplification Under Parameter Sign Inversions
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Structural Hysteresis in Directive-Gradient Systems: Thousand-Fold Amplification Under Parameter Sign Inversions
detail.abstract: We report systematic numerical investigation of parameter-sign inversions in directive-gradient field systems. Using fourth-order Runge-Kutta integration across five independent random initializations, we observe mean field-energy amplification of 1,096 ± 94-fold when the interaction parameter α is inverted from +1.2 to-1.2 during system evolution. This represents amplification approximately three orders of magnitude larger than the 9% thermodynamic difference between static equilibria initialized with opposite parameter values (hysteresis factor H = 1,005). The effect arises from structural memory: spatial correlation patterns formed under cooperative dynamics (α > 0) become thermodynamically incompatible local maxima when parameters invert to competitive regime (α < 0), triggering reorganization that converts accumulated structural potential into kinetic energy. Counterintuitively, gradual parameter interpolation increases amplification to 1,542 ± 168-fold by prolonging system residence in weakly-constrained intermediate states. Grid-independence validation (32 × 32 to 128 × 128), time-step sensitivity analysis (∆t = 0.005 to 0.020), and coefficient-of-variation reproducibility (8.6%) establish robustness. Results prescribe quantitative bounds on parameter-modification safety for gradient-following autonomous systems, where static equilibrium testing fundamentally underestimates operational transition risk.

detail.abstract: Malaysia's successful 2025 ASEAN Chairmanship culminated in the 47th ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur (October 26-28, 2025), delivering key economic advancements amid global trade tensions. Notable outcomes include the substantial conclusion of negotiations for the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) poised to potentially double the regional digital economy to US$2 trillion by 2030 upgrades to the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA), and enhancements to the ASEAN-China FTA. These achievements, alongside bilateral deals such as U.S. tariff exemptions on over 1,700 Malaysian products, have bolstered investor confidence, contributed to ringgit appreciation (to around RM4.05/USD by late December 2025), and reinforced tourism momentum ahead of Visit Malaysia Year 2026 (targeting 35.6 million international visitors). Malaysia recorded robust GDP growth of approximately 4.7-5.0% in 2025 (with Q3 at 5.2%), with projections easing to 4.0-4.3% in 2026 due to external risks. This article analyzes the Summit's economic implications for Malaysia, emphasizing sustained resilience in manufacturing, digital transformation, and regional trade.

detail.abstract: This study examines the role of green accounting, green auditing, and environmental consulting services in enhancing entrepreneurial sustainability and environmental performance in resourceconstrained regions. Using a balanced panel dataset of 150 enterprises in the Republic of Karakalpakstan over the period 2019-2024 (900 observations), the paper applies fixed-effects and instrumental-variable two-stage least squares (IV-2SLS) estimations to address endogeneity in consulting service adoption. Environmental performance is measured through a composite Environmental Performance Index (EPI). The results demonstrate that external environmental consulting exerts the strongest positive and statistically significant impact on ecological efficiency, exceeding the effects of internal green accounting systems and green audit practices. After correcting for endogeneity, the estimated impact of consulting services increases substantially, confirming that conventional models underestimate their true effect. The findings provide robust empirical justification for regional policy interventions, including green consulting vouchers and digital advisory platforms for small and medium-sized enterprises. The study contributes to the literature by offering one of the first econometric evaluations of green consulting effectiveness in Central Asia.

title: Construction of Sustainable Investment Equity Portfolios using Fitness Scores
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Construction of Sustainable Investment Equity Portfolios using Fitness Scores
detail.abstract: In this paper, we explore the shortcomings and practical implications of integrating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria in investment processes and develop a data-driven model for constructing diversified investment portfolios based on companies' sustainable revenue exposure. Our approach maximizes the portfolio diversification, considers a predetermined exposure of sustainable impact and determines industry weights in a portfolio optimization process using fitness scores. We implement fitness scores comprised of two fitness factors: companies' sustainable revenue exposure and the industry affiliation of the stocks. In our empirical study, we construct market-capitalization and equal-weighted sustainable investment equity portfolios. We analyze the characteristics of the portfolios such as risk and return profiles or the proportion of residual volatility and compare them to respective market/benchmark portfolios.

detail.abstract: In developing countries' innovation activities, limited patenting suggests structural gaps that hinder technological progress. This paper investigates whether countries can leverage their scientific and productive capabilities to realize untapped technological potential. We analyze connections between trade, science, and technology across global innovation ecosystems and introduce an indicator to assess where countries are positioned to expand their technological capabilities. Our results show that the indicator predicts technological output growth, though growth slows when countries exceed their predicted potential, indicating diminishing returns. The indicator performs better in more complex ecosystems. These findings provide valuable insights for policymakers, offering a framework to address weaknesses in innovation ecosystems and foster balanced, sustainable technological development.

title: The Impact of the Formula 1 Cost Cap on the Interplay Between Sporting Performance, Team Financial Outcomes, and Sponsor Engagement

detail.title: The Impact of the Formula 1 Cost Cap on the Interplay Between Sporting Performance, Team Financial Outcomes, and Sponsor Engagement
detail.abstract: This study examines how the introduction of the Formula 1 Cost Cap altered the relationship between team spending, sporting performance, and financial outcomes for teams and sponsors. Using panel data from 2015 to 2025, the analysis combines budget-performance regressions with an event-study approach to measure abnormal sponsor stock returns (AR, CAR). Event-study analysis reveals no statistically significant market reaction to sporting events in the post-cap period, confirming a decoupling of on-track success from immediate financial valuation. Concurrently, regression analysis shows a significant reduction in systematic risk (beta decreased by 10-34% for top teams) and a shift from scale-driven to efficiency-driven competition.

title: The Rationale for Presupposing Proxy Variables: Theoretical Deconstruction of the BKXY Framework and Supplementary Contributions to Nobel Prize-winning Research

detail.title: The Rationale for Presupposing Proxy Variables: Theoretical Deconstruction of the BKXY Framework and Supplementary Contributions to Nobel Prize-winning Research
detail.abstract: One of the core challenges in empirical economic research lies in the effective measurement of unobservable key constructs (denoted as X), such as "institutions" and "culture." The proxy variable method (with Y as the proxy variable) serves as the current mainstream solution, and its utility may be linked to an unformalized key parameter-the strength and direction of the association (K value) between the proxy variable and the core construct. This study develops the BKXY quantitative analysis framework to systematically establish a theoretical foundation for the validity of proxy variables. Findings suggest that deviations in the K value (K ≠ 1) may contribute to systematic biases in the estimation of causal effects (β), while misjudgments regarding the sign of the K value (e.g., misclassifying K < 0 as K > 0) are likely to reverse research conclusions. By reinterpreting the classic colonial origins study by Acemoglu et al. (2001), this research demonstrates the dual value of the BKXY quantitative analysis framework. Firstly, its diagnostic function indicates that the validity of the study's conclusions may not stem from the universal advantages of its econometric methods but rather from the stringent historical condition in the colonial context where the association strength (K) between "settler mortality" and "institutional quality" approximates-1. Secondly, its heuristic function reconstructs the original proxy variable as a measurement indicator for "institutional deficit," extending the research discourse from "whether institutions exert causal effects" to a new dimension of "the scale of institutional flaws and the urgency of remediation." Further analysis indicates that the K value issue may be widespread across disciplines, appearing in fields such as labor economics (e.g., "years of education" as a proxy for "human capital") and finance (e.g., "volatility" as a proxy for "risk"). Based on this observation, this study proposes a "normative practice guideline" that integrates theoretical justification of the K value, sensitivity analysis, and cross-validation into research design. The guideline aims to promote the evolution of empirical economic research toward greater rigor and transparency, offering a foundational methodological solution to address the discipline's replicability crisis.

title: Accounting for Under-reporting in Wildlife–Vehicle Collision Hotspot Identification Using Copulas and Bayesian Model Averaging
affiliations: Tongji University, Tongji University, Lund University, University of Massachusetts Lowell and Tongji University

detail.title: Accounting for Under-reporting in Wildlife–Vehicle Collision Hotspot Identification Using Copulas and Bayesian Model Averaging
detail.abstract: Wildlife-vehicle collisions (WVCs) pose significant risks to highway safety and wildlife populations, leading to considerable economic resources. However, efforts to systematically characterize and mitigate WVCs are often constrained by substantial under-reporting in official crash record databases. This study addresses these challenges using integrated police-reported and carcass removal data from thousands of road segments across roads of Washington State, USA. We propose a novel hybrid copula-based framework to jointly model reported WVC frequencies and under-reporting probabilities, incorporating Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA). In order to model WVC frequencies in segments of the highways, nine Poisson-mixed models were evaluated for reported WVC counts; the Negative Binomial (NB) provided the best fit, followed by Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial (ZINB) and Poisson-Weibull, with BMA posterior weights of 0.61, 0.23, and 0.16, respectively. The hybrid models link a binary logit under-reporting with the count submodel using Gaussian and Student-t copulas to capture dependence. To assess the model, we used the data of 7041 segments in the USA. The results illustrate that the key explanatory variables include traffic flow, truck percentage, roadway geometry, road type, and wildlife habitat indicators. The results shows that under-reporting probability decreases near wolverine habitat, on state routes, in low ecological value areas, and on roads with more lanes, but increases near white-tailed deer habitat and in the highest ecological value segments; reported WVC frequency increases with Annual Average Daily Traffic (AADT), wider average shoulders, proximity to large animal habitat, and higher speed limits, while it decreases with higher truck percentage, greater number of lanes, and poorer landscape connectivity. Empirical Bayes (EB) hotspot identification (HSID) shows copula-based models outperform independent specifications, capturing 2.4–3.9% more true collisions at selective thresholds (2–5%), with further gains from BMA. Residual diagnostics further confirm the framework’s robustness: hybrid BMA-copula specifications substantially reduce heteroscedasticity and alleviate remaining endogeneity bias compared to Gaussian, no-copula.

title: Pricing Wildfire Risk in Residential Real Estate: Invasive Grass-Fire Cycle
affiliations: and Zicklin School of Business, Baruch College - The City University of New York

detail.title: Pricing Wildfire Risk in Residential Real Estate: Invasive Grass-Fire Cycle
detail.abstract: We develop and implement an ex-ante, ecology-based measure of wildfire risk grounded in invasive grass proliferation and examine its impact on U.S. residential real estate, leveraging 40 million property transactions from 1991-2021. Using spatial data at the pixel level, we show that invasive grasses are associated with a significant increase in wildfire probability. Aggregating these predictions to the county level, we find that a 10% increase in predicted wildfire risk is associated with an average 2.6% (about $9,000) reduction in home values. These findings reveal that ecological degradation affects long-run asset values through a bi-directional grass-fire cycle, not just post-disaster losses. The results offer a new, market-based tool to assess and mitigate climate-related risks, informing asset pricing, insurance, and public investment strategies.

title: The Unintended Consequences of Interest Rate Caps on Small Dollar Loans

detail.title: The Unintended Consequences of Interest Rate Caps on Small Dollar Loans
detail.abstract: Interest rate caps on small-dollar loans could make it unprofitable for lenders to serve the market, restricting small-dollar loan access for borrowers and exposing them to unregulated alternatives. This study leverages a randomized controlled trial (RCT) implemented by a fintech lender in California and its Utah bank partner to assess these effects. Findings show no impact on loan take-up, and the caps lead borrowers to over-borrow from larger, unregulated loans when they restrict the small-dollar loan access. Without the interest rate cap, high-risk borrowers self-select into small-dollar loans, and the access to small-dollar loans can reduce their default rates. Heterogeneity analysis reveals greater benefits for financially fragile borrowers, especially low-income and underserved groups. Evidence shows that interest rate caps on small-dollar loans prevent borrowers from replicating favorable repayment schedules with larger loans, leading them to delay prepayment at a higher cost.

title: Municipal Nature Offset Markets – Balancing National and local Environmental Public Goods
affiliations: Center for International Climate and Environmental Research (CICERO)

detail.title: Municipal Nature Offset Markets – Balancing National and local Environmental Public Goods
detail.abstract: AbstractEnvironmental restoration, as a compensatory mechanism for the development of previously undisturbed land, can play a significant role in fulfilling nature conservation objectives. Numerous local authorities have adopted spatial planning frameworks that incorporate nature targets, such as “no net loss” (NNL), often operationalized through net area or net biodiversity principles (i.e., area neutrality or no net loss in biodiversity).  This study employs an analytical economic model to evaluate the welfare implications of both municipal offset schemes and coordinated offset strategies across adjacent municipalities, accounting for ecosystem services that also benefit local communities. Intermunicipal cooperation in achieving NNL targets can improve overall welfare compared to isolated municipal strategies. Nevertheless, offset markets may lead to an inefficient spatial distribution of net development across municipalities when local values of nature are heterogeneous. We suggest that implementing an offset market based on environmental value metrics, rather than strict area-based neutrality (ambient permits), may mitigate some of the inefficiencies inherent in area-neutrality frameworks.

title: The Inward Turn: From AI Outputs to AI Discourse

detail.title: The Inward Turn: From AI Outputs to AI Discourse
detail.abstract: Librarians have spent decades teaching students to evaluate sources, trace authority, and recognize how information is constructed. We’ve built sophisticated frameworks for this work. The advent of generative AI has obviously intensified these efforts. We’ve provided frameworks for evaluating AI-generated content: Is this output accurate? What biases might it contain? But as we've rushed to develop "AI literacy" programming, I wonder if we've overlooked a rich space where these same frameworks can be applied: the language we use to describe these systems in our own conversations, instructional materials, task forces, and workshops.

detail.title: An Analysis of Panic Buying Behavior and Retail Adaptation in Sri Lanka's 2022 Economic Downturn
detail.abstract: Sri Lanka's 2022 economic crisis trigged widespred consumer panic buying of essentials like rice, milk powder, and soap amid 70.2% inflation and severe shortages. This study examines retailer response strategies across formal chains and informal SMEs. Through literature review, it identifies gaps in understanding operational intermediation, economic crisis contexts , and formal informal retail differences. Key findings highlight. purchase limits, controlled pricing, transparent communication, and supply chain diversification as effective measures. Recommendations include quota systems for formal retailers, collective purchasing for SMEs, and policy support for crisis resilience, ensuring equitable goods access during Future shock.

detail.title: The Algorithmic Liquidity Trap: High-Velocity Swiping vs. Deep Engagement in Short-Video Platforms

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is based on theoretical modeling and numerical simulation; it does not involve human participants or animal experiments.
declarations.funderStatement: We acknowledge the financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 72450003).

detail.abstract: Short-video platforms balance user retention with high-frequency impression generation. We model this ecosystem using a Mean-Field Stackelberg Game with "traffic recycling," where users constantly re-enter the content pool. Solving the coupled HJB and Non-Local Fokker-Planck equations via a novel Spectral Soft Actor-Critic algorithm, we identify a critical "Algorithmic Liquidity Trap." While unconstrained optimization mathematically maximizes swipe flux, it drives dwell times to a physiological floor (τ ≈ 0.38s). We term this "Phantom Liquidity"-high throughput with zero effective economic value (violating IAB standards). Furthermore, we reveal a "Dopamine Treadmill" effect: improved content quality paradoxically increases user impatience, explaining the difficulty of sustaining long-form content. Our results demonstrate that without explicit constraints-such as weights for completion rates and creator interactions-algorithmic maximization inevitably collapses the ecosystem, validating the necessity of current industry governance structures.

detail.abstract: Keeping track of sample persons between waves of data collection helps minimize attrition in longitudinal studies. All things being equal, the longer the time between data collection waves, the greater the likelihood that sample persons have moved, and the greater the difficulty in locating movers (Couper & Ofstedal, 2007; Duncan & Kalton, 1987). In 1997, the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) changed from annual to biennial interviewing. To capture residential changes between waves, PSID began sending families a "contact information update" mailing in the year between data collection waves. Families who update or verify the address and telephone information and return it receive a $10 post-paid check. About half the families responded to this mailing in recent waves. During 2007, families providing this information needed far less tracking or refusal conversion efforts, and half as many contacts to be interviewed, underscoring the cost effectiveness of the mailing. Given these advantages, we designed a study before 2009 production interviewing to improve the response rate of the contact update mailing. Families were randomly assigned to the following conditions: $10 as a preversus post-paid incentive, mailing design (traditional versus updated), being sent a study newsletter, and timing and frequency of the mailing (July versus October versus both times). This paper reports on initial findings with regard to response rates to the mailing by these different conditions. Overall, there is no effect of incentive type implying that post-paid incentives are more cost effective. Traditional design performs better than updated design. Families receiving a second mailing have higher response rates than those receiving one mailing. There are some interaction effects with timing-of-mailing, with October-only families having higher response rates when also receiving a prepaid incentive and newsletter. Hypotheses for these findings and next steps for analysis are described.

title: AI Literacy Is Information Literacy: One Academic Library's Plan for AI Instruction
affiliations: Saint Francis University

detail.title: AI Literacy Is Information Literacy: One Academic Library's Plan for AI Instruction
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence, specifically Generative AI, is a topic that cannot be ignored in education, regardless of the level. As a library director at a four-year private university, I believe it is our duty as librarians to meet the challenge of AI head-on and meet the instructional needs AI creates. Using generative AI is a skill that both students and faculty should be trained in, including the proper uses of AI and how it can be used as a tool, while also being clear how to use it in a positive way. Libraries are uniquely positioned to do oversee this effort on college campuses, because AI literacy is information literacy, and librarians should lead.

title: From Burden to Premium: The Impact of Climate Transition Risk Exposure on Firm Value Based on Large Language Models
affiliations: Hunan University of Technology and Business, Hunan University of Technology and Business and Hunan University of Technology and Business

detail.title: From Burden to Premium: The Impact of Climate Transition Risk Exposure on Firm Value Based on Large Language Models
detail.abstract: Climate transition risk has emerged as a critical state variable reshaping the evolution of energy economic structures and the pricing of financial assets. However, consensus remains elusive regarding its microeconomic consequences and underlying mechanisms. Drawing on annual reports of Chinese A-share listed companies from 2010 to 2024, this study employs FinBERT and DeepSeek large language models to construct climate transition risk exposure indicators, systematically examining their impact on corporate value. When exposure remains below a critical threshold, compliance cost effects dominate. Accumulating regulatory burdens and rising expectations of asset stranding lead capital markets to apply valuation discounts. Beyond the inflection point, the innovation compensation effect, triggered by signals of deep transition, prompts the capital market to reprice long-term low-carbon competitive advantages, driving a rebound in firm value. Mechanism analysis reveals that shifts in institutional investors’ shareholding strategies and behavioral transitions in managerial overconfidence serve as key transmission channels for these effects. Heterogeneity analysis further demonstrates that the U-shaped pattern is more pronounced in firms with high customer concentration and insufficient green innovation, as well as in regions characterized by low physical risk, weak environmental regulation, or a lack of green financial support. This paper elucidates the nonlinear pricing logic underlying the transition of climate transition risk from a cost burden to a green premium, offering important insights for optimizing resource allocation efficiency and enhancing policy calibration precision during the energy transition.

title: Energy Price Sensitivity as an Asset Pricing Factor: Evidence from China’s A-Share Market
affiliations: Guizhou University of Finance and Economics, Guizhou University of Finance and Economics and Guizhou University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Energy Price Sensitivity as an Asset Pricing Factor: Evidence from China’s A-Share Market
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether exposure to energy price fluctuations constitutes a priced risk factor in the Chinese stock market. We construct a stock-level measure of energy price sensitivity based on an Energy Composite Index (ECI), which aggregates crude oil, coal, natural gas, and electricity prices using an iterative principal factor approach. Using data from China’s A-share market over the period 2014–2024, we examine the asset pricing implications of energy price sensitivity through portfolio sorting, Fama–MacBeth cross-sectional regressions, and multi-factor time-series models. We document a robust and economically significant negative risk premium associated with energy price sensitivity: stocks with higher exposure to energy price movements earn systematically lower expected returns. This result remains strong after controlling for firm characteristics and macroeconomic uncertainty measures. Industry-level analysis shows that the effect is particularly pronounced in energy-intensive sectors. Moreover, asymmetry tests indicate that the pricing of energy risk becomes stronger following sharp declines in energy prices, consistent with heightened investor reassessment of energy-related uncertainty. Overall, our findings provide compelling evidence that energy price risk represents an independent asset pricing factor in China’s equity market, with important implications for portfolio allocation and energy-related financial risk management.

title: Comparative Machine Learning Analysis for Employee Performance Prediction: Production-Ready Java EE System with Novel BLOB-Based Persistence
affiliations: Wilfrid Laurier University

detail.title: Comparative Machine Learning Analysis for Employee Performance Prediction: Production-Ready Java EE System with Novel BLOB-Based Persistence
detail.abstract: Inefficient employee performance management systems, which depend on subjective evaluations and lack the ability to predict future performance, cost corporations millions each year. This study details the design, execution, and rollout of an enterprise-level Employee Performance Analytics and Prediction System built on Java EE 8. This system fills important gaps between machine learning research and real-world application. Using a dataset with 17,417 employee records from Kaggle's HR Analytics repository, we tested three classification algorithm: J48 Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Naive Bayes using the Weka 3.8.6 machine learning library. Our empirical evaluation through 3-fold stratified crossvalidation demonstrates that Naive Bayes achieves optimal performance with 81.15% accuracy, outperforming ensemble methods. Atomic transactions, SQL-based model selection, and cluster-wide accessibility are made possible by the system's innovative BLOB-based model persistence mechanism, which addresses the stateless session problem present in enterprise Java environments. The system, which is deployed on a WildFly 18.0.1 application server with dual web service interfaces (JAX-RS 2.1 RESTful and JAX-WS 2.2 SOAP), exhibits production-grade performance: 142ms average prediction latency, sustained throughput of 35 predictions/second under concurrent load, and 99.7% uptime during 72-hour stress testing with 50 concurrent users executing 2,834 requests. This complete implementation demonstrates that enterprise Java EE platforms are still practical for contemporary machine learning deployments while giving businesses a standardsbased predictive analytics infrastructure.

detail.abstract: The Panel Study of Income Dynamics was born as a result of the desire to assess the success of President Lyndon Johnson’s War on Poverty on the economic well-being of U.S. families. In 1966 and 1967, the Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO) directed the U.S. Bureau of the Census to conduct a national assessment of the success of the War on Poverty by conducting a study called the Survey of Economic Opportunity (SEO), which completed interviews with about 30,000 households. Interest in continuing this national study led OEO to approach the Survey Research Center (SRC) at the University of Michigan about interviewing a sub-sample of approximately 2,000 low-income SEO households.

title: Post-Adoption Engagement with Non-Fungible Tokens: Motivational Orientations, Prior Experience, and Continuance Intention in Digital Commerce

detail.title: Post-Adoption Engagement with Non-Fungible Tokens: Motivational Orientations, Prior Experience, and Continuance Intention in Digital Commerce
detail.abstract: The global market for NFTs has gone through several boom-and-bust cycles and still remains a multi-billion-dollar market. But what are NFT buyers' aims in making these purchases? This study examines how motivational orientations and post-adoption experience jointly shape continued engagement with NFTs, using goal content theory (GCT) as a motivational lens. By applying the Aspiration Index (AI) to 1,075 participants, this study compares NFT buyers and non-buyers within a unified motivational framework. Wealth and community aspirations were modestly associated with prior NFT purchase experience and purchase intention, but these associations were substantially weaker than those linked to post-adoption experience. Prior NFT purchase experience showed the strongest association with purchase intention, consistent with post-adoption learning, usage reinforcement, and switching-cost explanations. These results challenge narratives that characterize NFT buyers as driven solely by speculation or fandom. Instead, they reveal a hybrid motivational landscape and suggest exposure to NFTs may reshape behavior, lending support to a technology adoption explanation. The study contributes to the literature on self-determined consumer behavior while offering actionable guidance for firms seeking to design successful NFT campaigns.

detail.abstract: Contemporary complex systems science is profoundly fragmented, lacking a unified axiomatic foundation to explain the very possibility of systems. This deficit becomes acute at systemic boundaries, from Gödelian incompleteness in mathematics and renormalization in physics, to control paradoxes in societies. Prevailing explanations remain ad hoc and phenomenological. We resolve this through a cross-disciplinary induction and a decisive logical reversal: instead of asking why systems fail at their limits, we inquire why stability is the norm. This reveals two constitutive principles of existence itself. The Principle of Spontaneous Organization posits an eternal, non-teleological tendency for systems to emerge from a potential field and sustain ordered structures against equilibrium. The Principle of Systemic Constraint asserts that any stable system must be equipped with self-governing metarules , which actively maintain coherence not by prohibition, but by dissolving the legitimacy of intrinsic threats like vicious self-reference through framework reconstruction. Together, these principles generate an eternal dynamical cycle-Potential → Emergence → Evolution → Collapse-that is universally nested across scales. This framework provides a unified ontological foundation for systems from particles to civilizations, radically recasting boundary crises not as failures, but as signatures of a deep, self-regulating existential logic. It heralds a paradigm shift from descriptive models to a dynamics of being.

detail.title: Let the Machine Read: Discovering New Topics with AI
detail.abstract: We present a robust topic modeling framework that mitigates overfitting while capturing the evolving nature of discourse. Our approach proposes a dynamic, temporal network-based model that adapts to emerging topics while maintaining semantic stability through alignment with predefined themes. To complement this adaptability, we introduce a static novelty detection method, catering to audiences favoring consistent topic structures. By balancing flexibility and stability, our framework enhances the interpretability and reliability of topic modeling in dynamic environments. Our findings significantly improve the capacity to monitor and analyze novel topics across various applications, including news tracking and social media analysis, ultimately providing a more robust framework for understanding the evolution of textual data over time. We apply our analysis framework on narrative from the Global Database of Events, Language and Tone (GDELT), filtered for the US presidential elections of 2024.

detail.abstract: 'Authorised push payment' (APP) scams involve a victim being tricked into transferring money to a fraudster. Catalysed by the rise of remote banking during the pandemic, this type of fraud has become an urgent problem, with some quarter of a million cases reported in the UK in 2023. ** In Philipp v Barclays Bank UK Plc [2023] UKSC 25 the Supreme Court rejected a claim brought by an individual account-holder against her bank for reimbursement of sums paid out as a result of an APP scam. Since Philipp, a 'world first' statutory scheme has been introduced in the UK, so that victims of certain types of APP scam will be now reimbursed by their banks. However, this scheme is limited in scope and the focus of this paper is the wave of common law claims relating to APP fraud since Philipp. Section 2 of the paper explains and contextualises Philipp and outlines the obstacles facing victims of APP fraud claiming for their losses on the basis of common law. Having done so, the discussion proceeds with two aims. The first, explored in section 3, is to examine how victims of APP fraud have sought to surmount various legal obstacles to common law claims in the two and a half years post-Philipp. The paper evaluates four strategies which have emerged to date and considers legal and policy themes running through them. The second aim of the paper, the focus of section 4, is a broader one, namely, to follow up the striking observations in Philipp about the role of courts and regulators in relation to the 'social problem' of APP fraud. This section explores the role of policy and legislation in the development of the common law and examines the approach of the courts adjudicating post-Philipp claims in the shadow of payment services legislation. This section concludes that the introduction of unprecedented legislative measures may have had a chilling effect on the common law. The law is stated at 24 October 2025.

detail.abstract: Registry systems have historically been understood as operational tools: mechanisms for collecting structured information to support service improvement, surveillance, clinical audit, and research. Over the past two decades, however, registries have expanded in scale, complexity, and methodological sophistication. They now underpin clinical quality systems, enable evaluation of real-world effectiveness, support learning health systems, and increasingly serve as foundational national data infrastructures. This article examines whether registry work can be considered a scientific discipline—registry science—and outlines the components required for such recognition. It further evaluates major methodological criticisms, examines ethical and socio-institutional contexts, and concludes with the implications for investment, training, policy, and standards of evidence.

title: Heterogeneous Individual Valuations of a Mild Climate
affiliations: University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics

detail.title: Heterogeneous Individual Valuations of a Mild Climate
detail.abstract: This paper has explored heterogeneous individual valuations of an important amenity, climate mildness, using a traditional Rosen-Roback empirical framework. It does so by including interaction terms between the amenity and worker characteristics in an hedonic wage regression that also include a housing-price measure. The results suggest that non-young workers (those in the mid-age and old groups) value a mild climate more than do young workers, matching the usual view that the tolerance for cold weather declines with age. The findings also suggest that, like their highly educated counterparts, workers with low education levels also highly value a mild climate, with workers in the middle range of education having a lower valuation. These findings, which contradict the view that only better-off individuals care about amenities, could reflect the lower burden in mild weather of the manual work done by the less educated. In addition to presenting these empirical findings, the paper further contributes by presenting new analytics for the Rosen-Roback model in a setting with individual heterogeneity.

title: Hitting Rock Bottom: Economic Hardship and Cheating
affiliations: Harvard University, , Charles University in Prague - Department of Economics and University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics

detail.title: Hitting Rock Bottom: Economic Hardship and Cheating
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether economic hardship undermines preferences for honesty. We use controlled, high-stake measures of cheating for private benefit in a large sample of 5,664 Kenyans, exploiting three complementary sources of variation: experimentally manipulated monetary incentives to cheat, a randomized increase in the salience of one’s own financial situation, and the Covid‐19 income shock (exploiting randomized survey timing, with respondents interviewed before vs. during the crisis). We find that cheating behavior is highly responsive to financial incentives in the experiment. Covid-19 economic hardship—marked by a 51% drop in monthly earnings—leads to a sharp increase in the prevalence of cheating, and the effect increases gradually with prolonged hardship. The effects are largest among the most economically impacted and are amplified when the salience of one’s own financial situation is experimentally increased. The results demonstrate that while most individuals exhibit a strong preference against cheating under normal conditions (in line with the existing body of work), economic forces can account for a substantial share of variation in dishonesty: the estimated cheating rate rises from 29% under low stakes in normal times to 86% under high stakes during the crisis.
